Norway's Sognefjord — the longest and deepest in the world — plunges to over 1,300 meters. The sea right outside a fjord's entrance is often much shallower than the fjord itself.

Shallow at the entrance. Here's a fascinating detail: the mouth (the opening where the fjord meets the open sea) is usually the shallowest part. This is because the glacier's power weakened as it reached the sea, so it carved less deeply there. This shallow ridge at the entrance is called a sill or threshold. It acts almost like a dam, trapping the deep, still water inside.

Steep walls on both sides. The sides of a fjord are not gentle slopes — they are dramatic, nearly vertical cliff faces or steep mountain walls. Waterfalls often cascade straight down these walls into the water below. The effect is visually stunning.

Calm, sheltered water. Because a fjord is enclosed on three sides with only a narrow opening to the sea, the water inside is remarkably calm. There are no crashing ocean waves. This makes fjords excellent natural harbors.

The water in a fjord is not purely saltwater. Freshwater constantly flows in from streams, rivers, rainfall, and melting snow trickling down the steep walls. This freshwater sits as a layer on top of the heavier saltwater below, creating distinct layers that don't easily mix. The deep, saltwater layer near the bottom can be very old — sometimes barely circulating at all — while the surface layer is fresher and more dynamic.

Fjords only exist where two things came together in the past: mountains meeting the sea and glaciers powerful enough to carve through them. Because of this, they are found in specific parts of the world:

  • Norway — the most famous fjord country in the world, with thousands of fjords along its western coast
  • Iceland and Greenland
  • Scotland (where they are sometimes called sea lochs)
  • New Zealand (in the Fiordland region — note the alternate spelling)
  • Chile (in Patagonia)
  • Canada (in British Columbia and the Arctic)
  • Alaska (USA)

Norway is so associated with fjords that the word itself comes from Norwegian. The Sognefjord in Norway stretches 205 kilometers inland and is considered the king of all fjords.
Fjord vs. Other Waterways — What Makes It Unique

People sometimes confuse fjords with other coastal features. Here's how a fjord is distinct:

  • A bay is wide and open. A fjord is long, narrow, and enclosed.
  • A river flows in one direction and carries fresh water only. A fjord is an inlet of the sea — the water flows in and out with tides.
  • A canyon is carved into dry land. A fjord is a glacier-carved canyon that has been flooded by the sea.
  • A lake is entirely enclosed by land. A fjord has an opening to the sea.

The single most important thing that makes a body of water a fjord and not just any inlet is its glacial origin — it must have been carved by a glacier. That's the test.

Beyond being spectacularly beautiful, fjords have practical importance:

  • Their deep, calm waters make them natural harbors, and many coastal towns and cities have historically been built at their edges.
  • Their protected waters support rich marine ecosystems, including fish, seals, and seabirds.
  • They are among the most visited natural landmarks in the world. Norway's fjords are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

If you had to capture a fjord in one sentence:

A fjord is a long, narrow, dramatically deep inlet of the sea, enclosed by towering cliffs or mountains, formed when a glacier carved a valley into the land and the sea later flooded it.
6129:
To flabbergast someone means to shock or astonish them so deeply and completely that they are momentarily left speechless, frozen, or unable to respond normally.

It is not mild surprise. It is not even strong surprise. It is surprise at its most extreme — the kind where your jaw drops, your mind goes blank, and you genuinely cannot find words for a moment.
How it differs from similar words

Think of astonishment on a scale:

Surprised → Shocked → Astonished → Flabbergasted

"Surprised" is the weakest. "Flabbergasted" is at the far end. When someone is flabbergasted, the shock hits them so hard that their mental processing essentially pauses. They are overwhelmed.

Compare:

  • "She was surprised by the gift." — mild, pleasant
  • "She was flabbergasted by the gift." — completely stunned, almost unable to believe it
Can it be positive or negative?

Both. Flabbergasted does not carry a built-in positive or negative meaning — it only tells you about the intensity of the shock. Context tells you the rest.

  • Positive: "He was flabbergasted when he won the lottery." (stunned with joy)
  • Negative: "She was flabbergasted when she discovered the betrayal." (stunned with disbelief and hurt)
  • Neutral/absurd: "I was flabbergasted that he'd eaten the entire cake by himself." (stunned by sheer ridiculousness)

The most natural and common form is "flabbergasted" (past tense / passive), used almost like an adjective to describe a person's state:

  • "I was completely flabbergasted."
  • "She stood there, flabbergasted."
  • "He looked flabbergasted."

It also works in the active form, where one thing or person flabbergasts another:

  • "The news flabbergasted everyone in the room."
  • "His audacity flabbergasted her."
  • "Nothing flabbergasts me anymore."

And as "flabbergasting" to describe something that causes this overwhelming shock:

  • "The results were absolutely flabbergasting."
  • "It was a flabbergasting discovery."

Flabbergast is an informal, conversational word. It has a slightly playful, expressive quality to it — people choose it not just to convey meaning but also to add colour and emphasis to their language. You would use it in everyday speech, casual writing, storytelling, or journalism. You would not typically find it in formal academic or legal writing.

Because of this expressiveness, it often appears with intensifiers:

  • "I was utterly flabbergasted."
  • "I was absolutely flabbergasted."
  • "I was completely flabbergasted."

These are very natural combinations.
The physical image the word carries

Part of what makes flabbergast so vivid is the physical picture it paints. When someone is flabbergasted, you can almost see it on their face: mouth open, eyes wide, a look of total disbelief. The shock is not just internal — it shows. This is why you will often see phrases like:

  • "a flabbergasted expression"
  • "a flabbergasted look on his face"
  • "she stared at him, flabbergasted"

To flabbergast someone = to shock and astonish them so completely that they are momentarily left speechless and stunned. It is the strongest form of surprise, can be positive or negative, is most commonly used in the passive form ("I was flabbergasted"), and carries an informal, vivid, expressive tone.
6130:
Flabbergasted means being so extremely surprised and shocked that you are left completely stunned — often speechless, wide-eyed, and unable to react or respond normally, even if just for a moment. It describes a state where something so unexpected has happened that your mind is momentarily overwhelmed by it.

Think of it like this: regular surprise is when someone jumps out and says "Boo!" Flabbergasted is when you walk into a room and discover 200 people threw you a surprise party you had absolutely no idea about. Your jaw drops. You can't find words. You just stand there. That is flabbergasted.

It helps to see "flabbergasted" on a scale of surprise:

Surprised → Astonished → Astounded → Flabbergasted

It sits at the very far end — the most intense zone. It is not just a little surprised, and it is not even simply very surprised. It is the kind of surprise that momentarily short-circuits your ability to think, speak, or react. The feeling is so powerful that it almost has a physical quality to it — a mental jolt, a freeze, a gasp.
What Makes It Different From Similar Words?

Several words are close neighbors to "flabbergasted," and knowing the difference sharpens your understanding.

Astonished means greatly surprised, but you can still function. Astounded is a step stronger, implying the surprise is almost hard to believe. Flabbergasted, however, goes further — it carries the strong sense that the surprise has temporarily knocked your ability to speak or respond right out of you. You're not just surprised; you're stunned into silence or stillness.

Dumbfounded is the closest relative. It also means so shocked that you are left speechless. The key difference is tone. "Dumbfounded" sounds more neutral and serious. "Flabbergasted" has a slightly larger, more expressive, almost dramatic feel to it — it conveys the full, almost comical weight of the shock.

Gobsmacked (popular in British English) means essentially the same thing, but it is more slangy and casual. "Flabbergasted" is more widely understood and slightly more formal than gobsmacked, though still informal overall.
Can It Be Used for Both Good and Bad Surprises?

Yes — this is important. "Flabbergasted" does not carry a positive or negative meaning in itself. The word simply describes the intensity of the surprise, not whether the news was good or bad. Context tells you which.

For a happy surprise: "She was flabbergasted when she found out she had won the scholarship."

For an unpleasant shock: "He was flabbergasted to discover that his wallet had been stolen."

For a neutral but shocking moment: "The audience was flabbergasted by the magician's final trick."

In all three, the core feeling is the same: something happened that was so unexpected, so out of nowhere, that the person was stunned by it.

"Flabbergasted" is informal to semi-formal. You would use it comfortably in everyday conversation, casual writing, social media, news articles, and creative writing. You would generally avoid it in very formal academic writing or official reports, where "astonished" or "stunned" would be more appropriate.

That said, it is not slang. It is a fully accepted standard English word with a long history, and educated speakers use it freely without it sounding out of place.
How Is It Used in a Sentence?

"Flabbergasted" works almost exclusively as a predicate adjective — meaning it comes after a linking verb like was, were, felt, seemed, or similar. The most common patterns are:

Subject + was/were + flabbergasted + by/at + [the cause]

  • "I was flabbergasted by the news."
  • "She was flabbergasted at the size of the bill."
  • "We were absolutely flabbergasted by what happened next."

You can also use it without specifying the cause, when the context already makes it clear:

  • "He just stood there, flabbergasted."
  • "She read the letter twice, still flabbergasted."

Occasionally, you'll see it used as an adjective before a noun (called an attributive position), though this is less common:

  • "A flabbergasted crowd watched in disbelief."

Certain words naturally appear alongside "flabbergasted" to add even more emphasis. The most common ones are:

Absolutely flabbergasted — by far the most common pairing. It stresses the completeness of the shock.
"I was absolutely flabbergasted."

Utterly flabbergasted — similar to "absolutely," but sounds slightly more literary.
"She was utterly flabbergasted by the decision."

Completely flabbergasted — also common, emphasizes total overwhelm.
"He was completely flabbergasted."

Simply flabbergasted — used for a more understated but emphatic effect, often in a slightly humorous tone.
"I'm simply flabbergasted."
The Subtle Feeling Behind the Word

One thing that makes "flabbergasted" special is its expressiveness. When someone uses this word, they are not making a cold, clinical observation. They are conveying genuine, full-bodied astonishment. There is a warmth and a vividness to it — it paints a picture of someone who literally cannot find their words because the surprise was that big.

Because of this, "flabbergasted" is a word that shows emotion, not just labels it. Saying "I was surprised" tells someone a fact. Saying "I was flabbergasted" makes them almost feel how overwhelmed you were. That is why skilled writers and speakers reach for this word when they want to communicate not just what happened, but how staggering it truly felt.

Flabbergasted = so extremely surprised and shocked by something unexpected that you are momentarily stunned, speechless, or unable to react normally. It is the highest level of surprise you can express with a single adjective in English. It works for good news, bad news, or neutral shocks. It is informal but not slang. It almost always follows a verb like was or were, and is commonly paired with words like absolutely or utterly for extra emphasis.
6131: Flabby describes something that is soft, loose, and lacking firmness — when it should ideally be tight, toned, or strong. Think of flesh that jiggles, wobbles, or sags when it moves. That is the image the word "flabby" paints.
Meaning 1: Physical / Literal (The Most Common Use)

When used to describe a person's body or a body part, flabby means the flesh is soft, loose, and out of shape — typically because of excess fat or a lack of muscle tone underneath.

Examples:

  • "After months of no exercise, his arms had become flabby."
  • "She wanted to tone her flabby stomach before summer."
  • "The wrestler's once-powerful thighs had grown flabby in retirement."

The key idea here is a contrast with what is expected or was once true. Flabby flesh doesn't feel solid when you press it — it gives way easily, like soft dough. It doesn't hold its shape. It may hang or droop. A flabby belly isn't just a big belly — it is a soft and wobbly one.

This is why the word is mildly negative and even insulting when used about a person. It isn't just saying someone has extra weight; it is saying their body lacks firmness and tone. Use it carefully, as it can feel unkind when directed at a real person.

Quick mental image: Imagine poking a firm, ripe apple vs. an overripe, soft one. The overripe one gives in — that softness and lack of resistance is what "flabby" captures about flesh.
Meaning 2: Figurative / Abstract (Used Beyond the Body)

"Flabby" is also widely used in a non-physical sense, and this is where it becomes a truly powerful and precise word. In this sense, it means something is weak, loose, limp, or lacking the strength and tightness it should have.

This can apply to:

Ideas and arguments:

  • "The lawyer's case was flabby — full of vague claims and no solid evidence."
  • "His reasoning was flabby; he kept going in circles without reaching a point."

Here, "flabby" means the argument has no firm backbone. Just like flabby flesh lacks muscle, a flabby argument lacks logical structure and strength.

Writing and language:

  • "The editor told her that her essay was flabby and needed tightening."
  • "Cut the flabby sentences and get to the point."

A piece of writing is "flabby" when it is padded with unnecessary words, repetition, or vague language — when it should be tight, lean, and precise. This is the opposite of crisp, sharp writing.

Organizations and leadership:

  • "Decades of comfort had made the company flabby and slow to change."
  • "The team's flabby management meant decisions took weeks instead of hours."

An organization is "flabby" when it has become bloated, inefficient, and lacking the energy or discipline to perform well.

The thread connecting all uses: Whether it's a body, an argument, a paragraph, or a company — "flabby" always means something that lacks the firmness, tightness, and strength it should have.
What "Flabby" Implies (The Feel of the Word)

"Flabby" doesn't just describe a state — it carries a sense of decline, laziness, or neglect. It suggests that something was (or could be) better, but has become soft and weak due to lack of effort, discipline, or care. This is what separates it from neutral words like "soft."

  • Soft is neutral — a pillow is soft, and that's fine.
  • Flabby is inherently negative — it suggests something has gone wrong.

Like most adjectives, "flabby" has comparative and superlative forms:

  • Flabby → "His arms are flabby."
  • Flabbier → "His arms are flabbier than they were last year."
  • Flabbiest → "That was the flabbiest speech I've ever heard."

Knowing the related forms of "flabby" will help you use it more flexibly:

  • Flab (noun) — The actual soft, loose flesh itself. "He wanted to lose the flab around his waist." It can also be used figuratively: "There's too much flab in this report."
  • Flabbiness (noun) — The quality or state of being flabby. "The flabbiness of his excuse was embarrassing."
  • Flabbily (adverb) — In a flabby manner. "The organization responded flabbily to the crisis." (Less common, but correct.)

WordWhat it meansKey difference from "flabby"

FatHaving excess body weightAbout size/weight; "flabby" is about texture and tone
LooseNot tight or firmly attachedMore about fit/structure than texture
SaggyHanging down looselyMore about shape and gravity; "flabby" is more about texture

Flabby means soft, loose, and lacking the firmness or strength that should be there — whether describing body flesh, an argument, writing, or an organization.

Master that one idea, and you will always use and understand this word correctly.
6132:
Imagine a balloon that is fully inflated — it is round, firm, and holds its shape. Now imagine that same balloon with the air let out. It becomes limp, soft, floppy, and hangs loosely. That deflated balloon is flaccid.

"Flaccid" describes something that lacks firmness, tension, or strength — something that is soft and limp when it should be (or once was) firm and strong.
The Two Main Ways It Is Used

1. Physical / Literal Use

This is the most common use. Something physical is called flaccid when it is soft, weak, and unable to hold its shape or resist pressure — when it should normally be firm.

  • A flaccid muscle is one that has lost its tone and strength. It feels soft and weak when you press it. A healthy, active muscle feels tighter; a flaccid one feels like slack rubber.
  • A flaccid handshake is a weak, limp handshake — the hand feels like a dead fish, with no grip or firmness.
  • A wilted flower stem is flaccid — it droops and bends because it no longer has the internal stiffness to stand upright.

The key idea here is always the loss or absence of expected tightness or firmness. It is not just "soft" — it is soft in a way that signals weakness or failure to function properly.

2. Figurative / Abstract Use

"Flaccid" is also used to describe non-physical things — like ideas, arguments, writing, performances, or leadership — when they lack force, energy, conviction, or effectiveness.

  • A flaccid argument is one that is weak and unconvincing. It makes its point without any real power behind it. You can push against it and it collapses easily — just like a limp balloon.
  • Flaccid writing or prose is dull, lifeless, and without energy. It does not grip the reader. It just lies there on the page, going nowhere.
  • Flaccid leadership means leadership that is indecisive, passive, and lacking the strength to drive things forward.

In all these cases, the word carries the same feeling as the physical meaning: something that should have strength and drive, but doesn't.
The Emotional Tone of the Word

"Flaccid" is almost always mildly negative. It does not just describe softness neutrally — it implies disappointment or failure. A pillow is soft, but you would never call it flaccid, because a pillow is supposed to be soft. You call something flaccid when its softness or weakness is a problem — when it has failed to be what it should be.

This is what separates "flaccid" from simple synonyms like "soft." Soft is neutral. Flaccid carries a quiet judgment: this should be stronger, and it isn't.

In medicine, "flaccid" has a very specific and important meaning. Doctors speak of flaccid paralysis, which is a type of paralysis where the muscles become completely limp and unresponsive. The muscles lose all tone — they cannot contract at all. This is contrasted with spastic paralysis, where muscles become stiff and tight. So in medical language, flaccid specifically means the muscles have no resistance or tension whatsoever.

Understanding nearby words will sharpen your sense of "flaccid":

  • Limp — very close in meaning; describes something that hangs loosely and has no stiffness. Flaccid is slightly more formal and often implies a greater degree of weakness.
  • Flabby — soft and loose, often used for flesh or muscle tissue that has lost its firmness.
  • Slack — not pulled tight; loose. A slack rope has no tension in it.
  • Lax — loose, not firm or strict. Often used for discipline, rules, or muscles.
  • Feeble — very weak, lacking power. More often used figuratively.
  • Languid — slow and lacking energy or enthusiasm.
• Firm, taut, toned, rigid, vigorous, forceful, strong

DimensionWhat "flaccid" means
PhysicalSoft, limp, lacking firmness or muscle tone
FigurativeWeak, unconvincing, lacking energy or force
Emotional toneMildly negative — implies failure to be strong enough
MedicalMuscles that are completely limp and unresponsive
One Final Way to Remember It

Think of the word "flaccid" as the opposite of the word "taut." Taut means pulled tight, firm, and under tension. Flaccid means the tension is gone — everything has gone soft and given way. Whenever you see or use "flaccid," picture that deflated balloon: it had shape, it had strength, and now it has neither.
6133: The word "flag" has several distinct meanings depending on the context. A flag is something that marks, signals, or represents — but what exactly it looks like and what it does changes quite a bit across different uses. Here is every major meaning explained clearly.
1. A piece of cloth that represents a country, group, or idea

This is the meaning most people know first. A flag, in this sense, is a rectangular (or sometimes differently shaped) piece of fabric with a specific design — particular colors, patterns, and symbols — that stands for something. It is a visual identity.

  • The Indian tricolor (saffron, white, and green, with the Ashoka Chakra) is India's national flag.
  • A sports club, school, or company might have its own flag.
  • A pirate ship traditionally flew a black flag with a skull and crossbones.

Flags of this kind are usually attached to a pole and displayed in visible places — outside buildings, on ships, or carried in processions. When a national flag is flown at half-mast (halfway down the pole rather than at the top), it is a sign of mourning or respect, usually after someone important has died or a tragedy has occurred.
2. A signal flag — a tool for communication

Long before phones and radios existed, flags were one of the primary ways humans communicated over distances, especially at sea. Different flags, or the same flag held in different positions, each carried a specific message. Sailors would spell out words or send coded signals using a set of signal flags — this system is called flag semaphore.

Even today, flags serve as live, real-time signals in many settings:

In motor racing (like Formula 1):

  • Checkered flag (alternating black and white squares) — the race is over; the winner has crossed the finish line.
  • Yellow flag — danger ahead; slow down, no overtaking.
  • Red flag — stop immediately; the race is being halted.
  • Black flag (shown to a specific driver) — that driver must come into the pits, usually as a penalty.
  • Blue flag — a faster car is approaching from behind; move aside.

In other areas:

  • A white flag is universally recognized as a sign of surrender or a desire for peace.
  • In scuba diving, a red-and-white diver-down flag is placed in the water to warn nearby boats that divers are below the surface.
  • In American football, referees throw a small yellow flag onto the field to indicate that a foul has been committed.
3. A small physical marker used to mark a location

A flag doesn't always have to be large. In everyday practical use, a "flag" can be any small marker — often a tiny piece of fabric or plastic on a stick — that is placed somewhere to draw attention or mark a specific spot.

  • In golf, a flag (also called the pin) is placed inside the hole on each green. Since the hole itself is tiny, the flag sticking up from it allows players to see where to aim from a great distance.
  • Surveyors and construction workers stick small colored flags into the ground to mark property boundaries, corners, or the locations of buried pipes and electrical cables — so that workers know exactly where to dig and where not to.
  • In the United States, many mailboxes have a small red flag on the side. When a resident has outgoing mail inside the box, they raise this flag as a signal to the postal carrier to stop and collect it.

"A flag" — especially a red flag — has become a widely used expression meaning a warning sign: something that suggests danger, a problem, or that something is not right. This meaning is borrowed from the world of racing and signaling, where a red flag literally means "stop, danger."

  • "The fact that he never showed up on time was a red flag."
  • "The doctor noticed a few flags in the test results."
  • "Her story raised several red flags for the investigators."

When something "raises a flag" or "raises red flags," it triggers concern, suspicion, or caution. You are not literally waving a piece of cloth — you are signaling that something seems off.

In a slightly different but related sense, to say something is "flagged" (used as a noun too, like "a flag on your account") means it has been marked for attention, review, or action — the way you might physically stick a flag on something to say "look at this."
5. A flag in computing and technology

In software and programming, a flag is a variable — typically one that can only be in one of two states: on or off, true or false, 1 or 0. It works like a light switch inside a program.

When the flag is "on," the program behaves one way. When it is "off," it behaves another way. For example:

  • A debug flag: when turned on, a program prints out extra information that helps developers find and fix errors. When turned off, this extra information is hidden from normal users.
  • A feature flag: used to turn a new feature of an app on or off without changing the code. This lets developers release a feature to a small group of users first, to test it safely.

You will also see "flags" used as command-line options — short instructions you type alongside a program's name to modify how it runs. For example, typing ls -a on a computer uses the -a flag to tell the program to show hidden files too. These are called flags because, like a physical flag, they signal a specific instruction.

In written sheet music, a flag (sometimes called a hook or a tail) is the small curved line attached to the vertical stem of a note. It tells the musician how quickly that note should be played — specifically, how short its duration is.

  • A quarter note has no flag (it gets one full beat in common time).
  • An eighth note has one flag (half the duration of a quarter note).
  • A sixteenth note has two flags (half again as short).
  • A thirty-second note has three flags.

The more flags a note has, the shorter and faster it is. When two or more of these short notes appear next to each other, the flags are often replaced by a solid horizontal beam connecting their stems — but individually, each is still said to have one or more "flags."
7. A flagstone — a flat paving stone

The word "flag" (often "flagstone" in full, but commonly shortened to just "flag") also refers to a large, flat, smooth slab of stone used to pave walkways, patios, garden paths, courtyards, or floors inside old buildings.

  • "The courtyard was paved with smooth grey flags."
  • "They laid new flagstones along the garden path."

These stones are typically cut or split from types of rock like sandstone or slate, which naturally form flat layers.

In the newspaper world, the flag (also called the nameplate) is the section at the very top of a newspaper's front page where the newspaper's name is displayed in large, distinctive lettering, along with the date, the edition, and sometimes the price. It is the paper's most visible branding.

  • The New York Times flag is its famous gothic-font title at the top of every front page.

This use is specialized to the world of print journalism, but you will encounter it if you ever study media or publishing.

At the heart of almost every meaning of "flag" is the same idea: something that signals, marks, or represents. Whether it's a nation's cloth banner on a pole, a tiny stick in the ground marking a buried cable, a red flag thrown by a referee, a true/false switch inside a program, a curved line on a musical note, or a warning sign in everyday speech — a flag is always something that says: look here, this means something, or pay attention to this.
6134: "Flag" as a verb has three distinct core meanings. They may seem unrelated at first, but once you understand each one with clear examples, you'll recognize them instantly in any context.
Meaning 1: To Mark Something for Special Attention

This is the most common and widely used meaning today. When you flag something, you mark it — physically or digitally — so that it stands out and doesn't get missed or forgotten. The idea is simple: you are placing an invisible "look at this!" sign on something.

Examples:

  • She flagged the email as important so she wouldn't forget to reply.
  • The editor flagged several errors in the report for the writer to fix.
  • The bank's system automatically flagged the transaction as suspicious.
  • Can you flag that paragraph? We need to discuss it in the meeting.

Notice that the thing being flagged is something that needs to come back to someone's attention — a problem, a priority, a concern, or something unusual. You are essentially saying: "Don't overlook this."

This meaning is also used when you bring something to someone's attention verbally or in writing, not just by marking it:

  • I just wanted to flag this issue before it becomes a bigger problem.
  • He flagged his concerns to the manager.

Here, "flag" means "to raise" or "to point out." You are drawing someone's eye toward something important.
Meaning 2: To Signal Someone to Stop (Usually "Flag Down")

This meaning is more physical and visual. To flag someone — or more commonly, to flag someone down — means to wave at them or signal them with your hand (or an actual flag) to make them stop or come to you.

Examples:

  • She ran to the roadside and flagged down a taxi.
  • The police officer flagged down the speeding car.
  • He tried to flag down a passing truck for help.
  • I flagged the waiter down to ask for the bill.

The core idea here is getting someone's attention through a visible signal so that they stop or come over. Think of it like waving a flag in front of someone's face — you can't ignore it.

In sports, especially American football, referees literally throw a yellow flag onto the field to signal a rule violation. So you might hear:

  • The referee flagged the player for holding.

This usage is a direct extension of the same idea — a visible signal that something must stop or be addressed.
Meaning 3: To Become Tired, Weak, or Less Energetic

This is a completely different and slightly older meaning. When a person, their energy, enthusiasm, or effort flags, it means it starts to decline, fade, or lose its strength — like a flag drooping when there's no wind to hold it up.

This meaning is intransitive, meaning nothing is being done to anything. The subject itself is weakening.

Examples:

  • After six hours of hiking, the group's energy began to flag.
  • His enthusiasm for the project flagged when he realized how much work it required.
  • The conversation flagged as they ran out of things to say.
  • She started strong, but her concentration flagged in the final hour of the exam.
  • Interest in the show flagged after the second season.

The key feeling this word captures is not a sudden stop, but a gradual decline — something that was going well or strongly starts to slow down, weaken, or lose momentum. It often suggests that the person or thing is struggling to maintain its earlier level of energy or intensity.
How to Tell the Three Meanings Apart

Since all three are spelled the same, context is everything. Here's a simple guide:

If someone is marking something (an email, a document, a problem, an error) → Meaning 1 (marking for attention).

If someone is waving at a person or vehicle to stop → Meaning 2 (signaling to stop), often with the word "down" after it.

If something is describing a loss of energy, enthusiasm, or pace — and nothing is being done to an object — → Meaning 3 (becoming tired or weak).
The One Thread That Connects All Three

Interestingly, all three meanings share a subtle common thread: drawing attention to something that is changing or needs to change. Whether you are marking a problem that needs attention, signaling a vehicle to stop, or describing energy that is falling away — in every case, "flag" points to something that is shifting, slowing, or standing out from the normal flow.

Recognizing that thread will help you internalize this word deeply, not just memorize it.
6135: To flagellate someone means to whip or beat them repeatedly — usually with a whip, a rod, a strap, or a similar instrument. It is not a casual or accidental act. The word always implies a deliberate, forceful, repeated striking. Think of it as a more formal, precise, and intense way of saying "to flog."

This verb is used in two distinct ways: literally (physical) and figuratively (emotional/mental).

Sense 1: The Literal (Physical) Meaning

In its most direct sense, to flagellate is to physically whip a person or animal with force. The act is prolonged and severe — not a single slap, but repeated lashing.

Examples:

  • "The cruel overseer flagellated the prisoners as punishment."
  • "Historical records describe how the soldiers flagellated condemned men before execution."

This sense appears most often in historical writing, religious texts, and descriptions of punishment or torture. You are unlikely to encounter it in casual, everyday conversation because the act itself is extreme and rare in modern life.

Sense 2: The Figurative (Self-Critical) Meaning — The More Common Modern Use

In modern English, the word is used far more often figuratively, and almost always in the reflexive form: to flagellate oneself, or the related noun self-flagellation.

Here, it means to punish, blame, or criticize yourself harshly and repeatedly — to mentally beat yourself up over something. Just like the physical act involves repeated, painful lashing, the figurative act involves repeated, painful self-criticism or guilt.

Examples:

  • "He spent years flagellating himself over the mistake, even though no one else blamed him."
  • "There's no use flagellating yourself about the past — what's done is done."
  • "She refused to flagellate herself for a decision she made with the best information she had at the time."

The key idea here is excess and repetition. You don't use "flagellate" for mild regret. You use it when the self-criticism is intense, prolonged, and arguably more painful than the situation deserves. It carries a tone of something almost self-destructive — as if the person is punishing themselves far beyond what is reasonable or helpful.
An Important Nuance: Why "Flagellate" and Not Just "Blame"?

The word "flagellate" is stronger and more vivid than words like blame, criticize, or reproach. When you say someone is flagellating themselves, you are communicating:

  • The self-criticism is intense, not mild.
  • It is repeated, not a one-time thought.
  • It may be excessive — more than the situation warrants.
  • It feels almost self-inflicted suffering — as if the person is hurting themselves on purpose.

This makes it a powerful word for describing someone trapped in a cycle of guilt or harsh self-judgment.

It is worth knowing that flagellation has a well-known historical and religious context, because you will encounter this in books and articles. In certain religious traditions — particularly in medieval Christianity — followers would physically whip or beat themselves as an act of penance, devotion, or atonement for their sins. Groups of people who practiced this were called Flagellants. This is directly where the figurative meaning of "punishing oneself" evolved from — the image of voluntarily suffering pain as a form of guilt and repentance is the same underlying idea, just moved from the body to the mind.
Who Uses This Word, and When?

• Writers and journalists use it figuratively when describing politicians, public figures, or ordinary people who engage in excessive guilt or self-blame.
  • Psychologists and therapists may use "self-flagellation" when describing unhealthy patterns of self-criticism.
  • Historians and scholars use it literally when writing about punishment, torture, or religious practices of the past.

It is not a word for everyday small talk. It is a formal, literary word. When someone uses it, they are deliberately reaching for something vivid and intense — they want you to feel the weight of the suffering, whether physical or emotional.
To flagellate is to whip or beat someone physically — and by extension, to punish or criticize yourself (or someone else) harshly, repeatedly, and excessively, as if inflicting deliberate pain.
6136:
Flagging describes something that is losing its strength, energy, or enthusiasm — something that was once going strong but is now noticeably weakening or slowing down.

Think of it like a fire that was burning brightly but is now dying down. The fire hasn't gone out completely, but it's clearly not as strong as it used to be. That "dying down" quality is exactly what flagging captures.

Two things must be true for the word to apply:

  1. There was a previous strength or activity. You can only flag if you were going well before.
  2. That strength is now visibly declining. It's not gone — just weakening.

This is important. You would never call something "flagging" if it was always weak. The word always implies a drop from a better state.
What kinds of things can be flagging?

The adjective is very flexible. It can describe anything that runs on energy, enthusiasm, momentum, or interest:

  • Energy / stamina — "After five hours of work, his energy was flagging." (He started strong but is now getting tired.)
  • Interest / attention — "The teacher noticed the students' flagging attention." (They were engaged at first, but now they're drifting.)
  • Enthusiasm / motivation — "Her flagging enthusiasm for the project was obvious." (She was once excited; now she's not.)
  • Morale / spirits — "The coach's speech lifted the team's flagging spirits." (The team had lost its fighting spirit.)
  • Sales / economy — "The company launched a new product to rescue its flagging sales." (Sales were good before but have been declining.)
  • Support / popularity — "The politician tried to win back his flagging support." (He had more supporters in the past.)
  • A conversation — "He cracked a joke to revive the flagging conversation." (The conversation had started well but was losing its flow.)
  • A career / performance — "She made a comeback after years of a flagging career." (Her career had declined from its earlier heights.)

Flagging has a slightly concerned or worried tone to it. When you describe something as flagging, you're not just noting a fact — you're signalling that the decline is a problem that someone may want to address. Notice how the example sentences above often include someone responding to the flagging thing — boosting it, rescuing it, reviving it. That's the natural companion to this word.

Flagging describes a gradual, ongoing weakening — not a sudden collapse. It's more like a slow leak than a burst pipe. The thing still exists and still functions; it's just operating below its earlier level and heading in the wrong direction.
Words close in meaning (and how flagging differs)

• Waning — very similar, but waning often sounds more poetic and natural (like the waning moon). Flagging feels more active and urgent.
  • Fading — implies something is becoming faint or disappearing, sometimes permanently. Flagging is more about losing drive or force.
  • Declining — more neutral and formal, often used with numbers or statistics. Flagging carries more emotional weight.
  • Lagging — means falling behind or not keeping pace with others. Flagging is specifically about losing one's own earlier strength, not about comparison to others.

Flagging = once strong, now visibly weakening.

Whenever you see this adjective, picture something that started with energy or momentum but is now running out of steam — and probably needs a boost.
6137:
Flagitious means deeply, outrageously, and shockingly wicked or criminal. It describes something so morally corrupt and villainous that it causes genuine horror or disgust in anyone who witnesses or hears about it.

Think of it this way: if "bad" is a one on a scale of moral wrongness, and "evil" is a nine, flagitious sits at the very top — a ten. It is not just wrong. It is horrifyingly, reprehensibly wrong.

Many words describe bad behavior — wrong, immoral, sinful, wicked — but flagitious is reserved for acts or people of the most extreme moral depravity. It carries two powerful ideas inside it at once:

  1. Serious criminality or villainy — acts that aren't just morally questionable, but deeply, gravely wrong, often on a large scale.
  2. Scandalous notoriety — the kind of wrongdoing that becomes publicly infamous, that shocks a community or society, not just one person.

So the word implies that the wrongdoing is both severe in nature and notorious in its impact. A petty lie is not flagitious. A dictator who orders mass atrocities and becomes infamous for them — that is flagitious.

The word can describe both people and actions/behavior:

  • A person can be flagitious — meaning they are a deeply wicked, villainous individual whose character is defined by serious moral corruption.
  • An act, deed, crime, or conduct can be flagitious — meaning the action itself is outrageously wicked, criminal, or disgraceful.

Here are clear examples showing how the word is used:

  • "The warlord's flagitious crimes against civilians were condemned by the entire world."
    His crimes were so horrifying and severe that they shocked everyone.
  • "She was a flagitious ruler who tortured her own people and enriched herself at their expense."
    She was a person of extreme, scandalous wickedness in her role of power.
  • "The flagitious behavior of the corrupt officials destroyed all public trust in the government."
    Their behavior was not just dishonest — it was outrageously, deeply immoral.
  • "History has recorded his flagitious deeds in painful detail."
    His acts were so seriously wicked that they became a notorious, documented part of history.

Flagitious is a formal, literary word. You will not typically hear it in casual conversation. It belongs in:

  • Formal writing
  • Historical or political commentary
  • Literature
  • Legal or moral philosophy

When someone uses this word, they are making a very deliberate, emphatic moral judgment. Calling something flagitious is not a casual criticism — it is a serious, weighty condemnation.
How It Differs from Similar Words

Several words are close in meaning, but each has a slightly different flavor:

  • Wicked — general evil, but not as extreme or specific.
  • Heinous — comes closest to flagitious; describes something shockingly evil, but heinous focuses more on the act being deeply offensive to moral senses, while flagitious also carries a stronger sense of criminal guilt and public notoriety.
  • Nefarious — implies scheming, deliberate villainy (a nefarious plan), but doesn't necessarily carry the same sense of shocking scandal.
  • Atrocious — focuses on something being horrifyingly cruel or terrible in execution.
  • Iniquitous — means profoundly unjust and wicked, but is slightly more focused on injustice than on scandal.

Flagitious sits at the intersection of serious guilt + extreme moral depravity + notorious scandal. That combination is what makes it unique.

If you ever need to recall this word quickly: flagitious means so outrageously wicked and criminal that it is a matter of deep public shame and moral horror. It is the strongest, most damning adjective you can reach for when describing a person or act as genuinely, gravely, and notoriously evil.
6138: A flagon is a large container used for holding and serving liquids — almost always an alcoholic drink like wine, beer, or cider. Think of it as a big jug built specifically for drinking occasions, whether at a tavern table, a feast, or a gathering.

A flagon has a very recognizable shape. It typically has:

  • A wide, round body to hold a large volume of liquid
  • A narrow neck at the top
  • A handle on the side so you can carry or pour it easily
  • A lid or stopper to keep the contents fresh and prevent spilling
  • A spout or lip for pouring into cups

Picture a sturdy, old-fashioned jug with a lid — that is essentially a flagon. It is noticeably larger than a regular bottle or cup. A classic flagon holds roughly one quart (about one litre) or even more.

Flagons have been made from many different materials depending on the era and purpose:

  • Pewter or silver — very common in medieval and Renaissance times, especially for wealthy households and taverns
  • Ceramic or earthenware — thick, clay-based flagons were common and practical
  • Glass — more elegant, used for finer settings
  • Leather — yes, even hardened leather was used in older times for portable flagons

A flagon serves two main purposes:

1. Serving drinks at the table. A flagon would sit at the centre of a feast or tavern table, and people would pour from it into their individual cups. It is essentially a serving vessel — like a communal pitcher of drink.

2. Storing or transporting a large quantity of drink. Because of its size, a flagon is a convenient way to carry a good amount of liquid from one place to another — from a cellar to a table, for example.

In some parts of the world today, particularly in the United Kingdom and Australia, the word "flagon" is still used to refer to a large bottle of wine or cider sold commercially, usually holding around 2 pints (roughly 1.1 litres).

The bigness of a flagon is one of its defining features. It is not a personal drinking vessel (that would be a cup, mug, or goblet). It is a shared or bulk vessel — something that contains enough drink to fill multiple cups. When you see the word "flagon," always picture something sizeable and abundant.
How It Differs from Similar Things

Since learners often confuse similar words, here is a clear breakdown:

  • Flagon vs. Flask — A flask is small, personal, and portable (something you slip into a pocket). A flagon is large and meant to sit on a table or be carried by hand.
  • Flagon vs. Jug — A jug is open-topped with no lid. A flagon typically has a lid or stopper.
  • Flagon vs. Decanter — A decanter is a refined, usually glass vessel used to pour wine elegantly. A flagon is more robust and rustic, built for volume rather than elegance.
  • Flagon vs. Barrel/Cask — A barrel is enormous and not for pouring at the table. A flagon is large but still human-sized and handleable.
Where You Will Encounter This Word

You will most commonly see "flagon" in:

  • Historical novels, medieval stories, or fantasy literature — characters in taverns often drink from flagons
  • The Bible — flagons appear in several passages, often referring to vessels of wine
  • Poetry and older English literature — it carries a rich, old-world feel
  • Everyday speech in some regions — especially in Australia and Britain, when referring to a large bottle of wine or cider
A Simple Picture in Your Mind

Imagine you are sitting in a stone-walled tavern in medieval England. The innkeeper walks over and places a large, pewter jug with a hinged lid on your wooden table. It is full of ale, enough for you and three friends. That container — sturdy, lidded, handled, and generously sized — is a flagon.
A flagon is a large, handled, usually lidded vessel designed to hold and pour a substantial quantity of a drink, most often an alcoholic one like wine, beer, or cider.
6139:
When something is flagrant, it means it is so obviously wrong, bad, or unacceptable that it is impossible to miss or ignore. It screams at you. It is a wrongdoing that is out in the open — not hidden, not subtle, not accidental — and often done with a shocking lack of shame.

Think of it this way: if a mistake or bad act is a small crack in a wall, a flagrant one is the entire wall crumbling in front of everyone.

The word flagrant always contains two ideas working together. If either one is missing, the word doesn't quite fit.

1. It must involve something wrong, bad, or against the rules.
Flagrant is never used to describe something neutral or positive. It is always attached to a violation, a lie, an injustice, an error, or a bad act.

2. It must be glaringly obvious.
The wrongdoing is not hidden or disguised — it is visible, clear, and striking. Anyone with eyes can see it. The person doing it isn't even trying to conceal it. This is what separates flagrant from just saying something is "bad." A flagrant act is conspicuously bad.

So flagrant = obviously and shamelessly wrong.
What Kinds of Things Can Be Flagrant?

Flagrant is almost always used to describe acts, behaviors, violations, or errors — not people or objects. Here are the most common things you'll see it paired with:

  • A flagrant violation — breaking a rule so openly that everyone can see it
  • A flagrant foul — in sports, a very obvious and serious foul, often dangerous or intentional
  • A flagrant lie — a lie so obvious that it insults the intelligence of the people hearing it
  • A flagrant disregard — completely ignoring a rule, a person's rights, or a duty, without even trying to hide it
  • A flagrant abuse — a very obvious misuse of power, authority, or trust
  • A flagrant error — a mistake so glaring that it is hard to believe it was made
  • A flagrant breach — an obvious breaking of an agreement, contract, or code of conduct

These examples will show you exactly how the word feels in use:

  • The soldier's actions were a flagrant violation of the ceasefire agreement — he fired shots in broad daylight in front of journalists.
  • The referee called a flagrant foul after the player deliberately elbowed his opponent in the face.
  • It was a flagrant lie — she said she had never met him, yet photos of them together were all over the internet.
  • The company showed flagrant disregard for worker safety by ignoring multiple government warnings.
  • The student copied the entire essay word for word — a flagrant act of plagiarism that even a child could spot.

Notice how in every example, the bad act is out in the open, undeniable, and often done as if the person doesn't care who sees it. That shameless, brazen quality is the heart of the word.

Flagrant is a strong word. It belongs at the serious end of the scale. You wouldn't use it for a small mistake or a minor rule-bending. It is reserved for things that are not just wrong, but glaringly, shockingly wrong.

Scale of severity:
Minor mistake → serious error → flagrant violation (this is near the top)

If someone tells a small white lie, you wouldn't call it flagrant. But if a politician lies about something that is disproved by video footage that everyone has already seen, that is flagrant.
How It Compares to Similar Words

Since you want to truly understand this word, it helps to see how it sits among words that are close to it in meaning.

Blatant is the closest synonym and can often be swapped with flagrant. However, blatant focuses more on the obviousness of something, while flagrant adds a stronger sense of moral wrongness and shock. You can say "that's blatantly obvious" in a neutral sense, but flagrant always implies something offensive or against the rules.

Egregious is also similar — it means outstandingly bad. But egregious focuses more on the extreme degree of badness, while flagrant focuses on the open, undeniable visibility of the bad act. Egregious is about magnitude; flagrant is about unmistakability.

Brazen means done shamelessly and boldly. Brazen is about the attitude of the person doing the act (doing it without shame). Flagrant describes the nature of the act itself (it's undeniably, visibly wrong). The two ideas overlap a lot, which is why flagrant acts often feel brazen too.

Flagrant is a somewhat formal word. You'll see it often in:

  • News reporting and journalism
  • Legal and courtroom language
  • Sports commentary (especially "flagrant foul")
  • Academic and political writing

You wouldn't commonly hear it in casual everyday conversation, though it wouldn't sound wrong there either. It simply carries a slightly serious, emphatic weight.
One Sentence to Remember It Forever

If you ever forget what flagrant means, come back to this sentence:

A flagrant act is so obviously and shamelessly wrong that there is no denying it, no hiding it, and no excusing it.

That is flagrant, in its entirety.
6140:
Imagine a navy with many warships sailing together as a group — this is called a fleet. Among all those ships, one ship is chosen as the most important one. The commanding officer (called an admiral — the highest-ranking person in the navy) lives and works on this special ship. It is the headquarters of the entire fleet. To let everyone know which ship the admiral is on, a special flag is raised on it.

That ship is the flagship.

So literally, a flagship is the most important ship in a naval fleet — the one that carries the commander and flies the identifying flag. Every other ship in the fleet follows the flagship's lead. It is typically the strongest, best-equipped, and most capable ship in the group.

Over time, people started borrowing this idea and applying it to things completely outside of ships and navies. Today, flagship is used far more often in this broader, everyday sense.

In modern usage, a flagship is:

The most important, most impressive, or best example of something within a group — especially a product, store, or project that a company is most proud of and uses to represent itself.

The logic is identical to the naval meaning. Just as the flagship ship was the best and most important in the fleet, a "flagship" product or store is the best and most important in a company's collection.

When something is called a flagship, it usually means:

1. It is the best version. It has the most features, highest quality, or greatest capability compared to others in the same group.

2. It is the most representative. It is what the company shows off to the world. If you want to know what a company is truly capable of, you look at its flagship.

3. It is the face of the brand. Other products or things in the group are less important, less advanced, or meant for different purposes. The flagship sits at the top.

4. It often gets the most attention and investment. Resources, effort, marketing — the flagship gets priority.

Technology:
A smartphone company releases many phones at different prices. The most advanced, most powerful, most expensive model with all the latest features is called their flagship phone. For example, a company might sell budget phones, mid-range phones, and then their top-of-the-line model — that top model is the flagship.

Retail:
A clothing brand has hundreds of stores around the world. But one store — usually the biggest, most beautifully designed, most fully stocked store in the most important city — is called their flagship store. It's where you see the brand at its absolute best.

Business/Organizations:
A university might run many programs and research centers. The one it is most known for, most proud of, and invests the most in, might be called its flagship program.

Products in general:
A car company might make many models. The most luxurious, most powerful, most expensive one — the one that sits at the top of their entire lineup — is their flagship model.
A Simple Way to Remember It

Whenever you see or hear "flagship," ask yourself: "Is this the best, most important, most representative thing in its group?" If yes — that's a flagship.

Think of it this way: the flagship is always the crown jewel. It's what the leader leads with. It's what the brand stands behind with the most pride.

• "The company unveiled its new flagship smartphone at the annual event." → Their best, most advanced phone.
  • "She visited the brand's flagship store in New York City." → The most important, grandest store the brand owns.
  • "Clean energy research is the flagship initiative of the organization." → The most important project they're known for.
  • "The hotel's flagship property is located in Paris." → Their best and most prestigious hotel.

A flagship is always the best within a specific group. A flagship phone is the best phone from that particular company — it doesn't necessarily mean it's the best phone in the entire world. A flagship store is the most important store for that brand — not necessarily the biggest store on earth. The word always implies a comparison within a defined group or brand, not a universal ranking.

In short: A flagship is the single most important, most impressive, most representative thing within a group — be it a ship in a fleet, a product in a lineup, or a store in a chain. It is what the group leads with and is most proud of.
6141: A flail is a tool — or sometimes a weapon — made of two sticks connected by a flexible joint (like a hinge, a leather strap, or a chain). The key feature is that the two parts are not rigidly attached. Instead, one part hangs loosely from the other and can swing freely, which is exactly what makes a flail useful.
The Agricultural Flail (The Original and Primary Meaning)

This is the oldest and most fundamental meaning of the word.

Imagine you've harvested wheat. The grain — the edible part — is still attached to the stalk. How do you get it off? You beat it. That's what a flail is for.

A farming flail has two parts:

  • The long handle — the part you hold in your hands. It can be as long as a walking stick or slightly longer.
  • The short striking stick — a heavier, shorter rod attached to the bottom of the handle by a flexible piece of leather or rope. This part hangs down and can swing in any direction.

When a farmer swings the long handle, the short stick at the end whips forward and smashes down onto a pile of harvested grain laid out on the ground. The beating knocks the grain kernels loose from the husks and stalks. This process is called threshing.

Because the connection between the two parts is flexible (not rigid like a single wooden stick), the short end builds up extra momentum as it swings — it almost "lashes" forward at the end of each swing. This is what makes the flail more effective for threshing than simply hitting with a single stick.

For most of human history — before machines existed — the flail was one of the most important farm tools in the world. Farmers would spend hours, even days, swinging flails over grain spread on barn floors.

Because the same swinging, whipping design that works so well for beating grain is also effective for hitting people, flails were adapted into weapons — particularly during the medieval period.

A weapon flail works on the same principle: a handle connected by a chain (instead of leather) to one or more heavy metal balls, sometimes covered in spikes. The chain lets the striking head swing with tremendous force, and the flexible connection makes it very difficult for an opponent to block with a sword — the head wraps around a blocking weapon and still strikes.

Weapon flails come in a few forms:

  • A one-handed flail: a shorter handle with a single spiked ball on a chain — a common infantry weapon.
  • A two-handed flail: a longer weapon for heavier strikes.
  • A morning star: sometimes called a flail, though some people distinguish between the two — it typically has a longer chain.

Whether it's a farm tool or a weapon, the thing that makes something a flail is always the same: two parts, connected flexibly, where one part swings freely and strikes with force. Remove that flexibility, and it's just a stick. The flexible joint is the soul of the flail.

Because of how a flail moves — swinging wildly, lashing out — the word is sometimes used figuratively to describe anything that strikes in a sweeping, uncontrolled, or thrashing manner. For example, a machine with wildly spinning parts might be described as working "like a flail." However, this figurative use is much more common with the verb form of the word ("to flail around"). In its noun form, "flail" almost always refers to the actual tool or weapon.

A flail is a two-part tool or weapon in which a shorter, heavier striking piece is attached by a flexible link to a longer handle, allowing it to swing freely and strike with whipping force — used by farmers to beat grain off stalks, and by medieval warriors as a difficult-to-block weapon.
6142: Flail means to move or wave wildly, without control — often in a frantic or desperate way. The key idea hiding inside this word is loss of control combined with frantic effort. Whenever you see or use the word "flail," those two things are almost always present: someone is trying, but they have no control over what they're doing.

1. Physical Flailing — the body moving wildly

This is the most visual meaning. When a person (or part of their body, like arms or legs) flails, it moves rapidly in all kinds of directions — up, down, sideways — in an uncoordinated, chaotic way. There is no grace, no precision, no purpose to the movements. It looks panicked and desperate.

Picture this: Someone slips on ice. In that split second before they fall, their arms shoot out in every direction — swinging, grabbing at air — as they desperately try not to fall. That frantic, wild arm movement? That is flailing.

More examples of physical flailing:

  • A child having a tantrum on the floor, arms and legs kicking and swinging everywhere, is flailing.
  • A swimmer in panic, thrashing their arms chaotically instead of swimming properly, is flailing.
  • A person on a tightrope losing their balance and swinging their arms wildly to recover is flailing.
  • Someone trying to swat a bee away by swinging their arms frantically in every direction is flailing at the bee.

Notice something they all share: lots of rapid, big movement — but zero control.

2. Figurative Flailing — struggling without direction or success

This is where the word gets even more useful in daily life. Flail is very commonly used in a non-physical, figurative way to describe a person, a team, or even an organization that is struggling badly, without a clear plan, and not making real progress. They are putting in effort, but it is disorganized, scattered, and ineffective — just like those wild arms.

Picture this: Imagine a student who gets placed in an advanced class they are not ready for. They don't understand the lessons. They try different things — they re-read notes, they guess on tests, they ask random questions — but nothing works. They have no real strategy. They are not improving. They are just... desperately spinning their wheels. That student is flailing.

More examples of figurative flailing:

  • A new manager with no experience who doesn't know how to lead their team is flailing in their new role.
  • A company losing customers rapidly, trying random fixes without a real plan, is flailing.
  • A politician who cannot answer questions clearly in a debate and keeps giving confused, off-topic answers is flailing.
  • A team that is losing badly and has no strategy left is flailing.

The figurative meaning always carries the same emotional weight as the physical one: panic, desperation, and a lack of control or direction. It paints a picture of someone who is not calmly problem-solving — they are scrambling.

This is important. "Flail" is not a neutral word. It carries a strong feeling with it. When you say someone is flailing, you are suggesting:

  • They are out of their depth (the situation is too much for them)
  • They are not in control
  • Their efforts are wasted or ineffective
  • There is an element of desperation or panic

Because of this, "flail" can sometimes sound slightly critical or pitying. Saying "he was flailing in that meeting" implies he was doing poorly and struggling visibly — it is not a compliment.
Subtle but Important: Flailing vs. Just "Struggling"

You might ask: "Isn't flailing just another word for struggling?" Not quite. Here is the difference:

  • Struggle simply means things are hard and someone is working through difficulty. It is neutral.
  • Flail adds the idea that the effort is wild, uncontrolled, and not working. There is an image of chaos and ineffectiveness baked into it.

A person can struggle to climb a mountain but do it with skill and composure. That same person flails when they lose their footing and grab desperately at rocks in a panic.
How "Flail" Is Commonly Used in Sentences

• "Without guidance, the new intern was clearly flailing."
  • "She flailed her arms to get the waiter's attention."
  • "He flailed in the water until the lifeguard reached him."
  • "The campaign began to flail after the candidate's poor debate performance."
  • "Stop flailing and make a proper plan."
  • "The toddler flailed his arms and legs in excitement."
To flail means to move or act in a wild, uncontrolled, and frantic way — whether that's your body thrashing about physically, or your efforts falling apart in a panicked, directionless mess.
6143:
"Flair" describes something special — a quality that goes beyond ordinary. It suggests that something is done (or possessed) in a way that feels natural, impressive, and a little bit extraordinary. It is always a compliment.

The word has two closely related meanings, and understanding both together will give you the complete picture.

When someone has a flair for something, it means they have a natural gift or an instinctive ability for it — the kind of talent that seems to come from within, almost effortlessly.

"She has a flair for languages."
"He has a flair for business."
"The child showed a flair for painting from a very young age."

What makes this different from just "talent" or "skill"?

This is the important nuance. All three words are related, but they aren't identical:

  • Skill is something you can build purely through practice. A robot could technically develop skill.
  • Talent is a natural ability — you're born with it.
  • Flair goes one step further. It suggests that the ability feels intuitive and instinctive — almost like a sixth sense. A person with flair doesn't just do something well; they seem to feel it naturally. There is a sense of ease and confidence in how they do it. It also carries a hint of creativity and originality — not just competence, but a personal, inspired touch.

Think of it this way: a trained cook can have great skill. But a cook with a flair for cooking somehow just knows what flavors to combine, adds an unexpected twist, and makes even simple food feel special.
Meaning 2: Stylishness and Originality in How You Do Something

The second meaning is about how someone does something — with energy, style, creativity, and a certain impressive confidence. This is often expressed as doing something "with flair."

"She dresses with flair."
"He presented the report with flair — everyone in the room was impressed."
"Even the way she entered the room had flair."

Here, flair means a kind of panache — a quality that makes something stand out from the ordinary. It's not just that the thing is done well; it's done with personality, creativity, or a distinctive spark. There is an element of being noticed, of leaving an impression.

These two meanings are deeply linked, which is why the word carries so much weight. When someone has a flair for something (Meaning 1), they often naturally do it with flair (Meaning 2). The inner gift expresses itself outwardly as style and originality. That's the beautiful double quality this word captures.
A Third Use: Describing the Character of a Place or Thing

"Flair" can also describe the distinctive feel or character of a place, a style, or a design — usually with an adjective in front of it.

"The restaurant had a distinctly French flair."
"Her apartment was decorated with a bohemian flair."
"The festival had a theatrical flair that everyone loved."

Here, flair means a distinctive, recognizable quality — a flavor or spirit that makes something feel unique and vivid.
A Very Common Phrase: "A Flair for the Dramatic"

This is one of the most widely used expressions with this word, and it deserves special attention.

"My sister has a flair for the dramatic."

This means the person tends to exaggerate situations, react in a theatrical way, or make things seem more intense or exciting than they really are. It's usually said with gentle amusement, not harsh criticism — it's describing a personality trait that makes life feel like a performance. It can be charming, entertaining, or sometimes exhausting, depending on context.

To sharpen your understanding, here's what the word does not mean:

  • It does not mean ordinary effort or hard work alone. A person who works very hard but produces average, unremarkable results would not be described as having flair.
  • It is not neutral. It is always positive and admiring.
  • It does not apply to negative abilities. You would never say someone has "a flair for lying" in a straightforward, admiring way — unless used sarcastically.
Summary in One Sentence per Meaning

• Meaning 1: A natural, instinctive gift for something that goes beyond mere skill — it feels effortless, intuitive, and creatively inspired.
  • Meaning 2: The quality of doing things with impressive style, originality, and confidence — in a way that stands out and leaves an impression.
  • Meaning 3: The distinctive, vivid character or feel of a place, design, or style.

All three meanings share one soul: something ordinary made extraordinary by a special, natural quality.
6144: "Flak" has two meanings — one literal and one figurative. The figurative meaning grew out of the literal one, so understanding the literal one first makes everything click.

In a military context, flak refers to gunfire shot upward from the ground to destroy enemy aircraft flying overhead. More specifically, it refers to the shells, explosions, and deadly fragments of metal (shrapnel) that burst through the air as those shells explode.

Picture this: during World War II, a bomber crew flies their plane deep into enemy territory on a mission. Below them on the ground, the enemy has powerful guns pointed at the sky. Those guns fire shells upward that explode in mid-air, filling the sky around the aircraft with bursting fire and flying metal fragments. That is flak — the whole dangerous cloud of exploding shells and shrapnel that the pilots had to fly through.

The guns that fire these shells are called flak guns. The exploding shells themselves, the fragments they produce, and the overall barrage of fire are all called flak.

What makes flak dangerous?

A single flak shell doesn't need to score a direct hit to cause damage. When it explodes mid-air, it shatters into countless razor-sharp metal fragments that scatter outward at high speed in all directions — like a shotgun blast, but enormous. A plane flying through intense flak is being pelted from every direction by these fragments, which can tear through the aircraft's body, engines, or fuel tanks, and wound or kill the crew.
2. The Figurative Meaning — Harsh Criticism or Hostility

In everyday modern language — and this is by far the more common usage — flak means strong criticism, disapproval, or hostile pushback directed at a person, organization, or decision.

When someone "catches flak," "gets flak," or "takes flak," it means people are attacking them verbally — criticizing them sharply, expressing loud disapproval, or opposing them aggressively.

Examples:

  • "The politician took heavy flak after announcing the new tax."
  • "The company is getting flak from customers over the price increase."
  • "She caught a lot of flak for speaking out against the decision."
  • "He had to face serious flak from both his critics and his own team."
How the Two Meanings Are Connected

The connection is really intuitive once you see it. Think of a bomber pilot flying through a sky full of exploding shells coming at them from all sides — dangerous, relentless, coming from multiple directions at once, and hard to escape.

Now think of a politician or a CEO who makes an unpopular decision and is suddenly bombarded with harsh criticism from journalists, the public, and opponents — all at once, from all sides.

The feeling is the same: being under attack, pelted from multiple directions, trying to get through it. So people borrowed the word "flak" to capture exactly that sense of being verbally bombarded.

a) Flak implies intensity and volume.
Calling something "flak" (rather than just "criticism") suggests the attacks are strong, sustained, or coming from multiple people at once. You wouldn't normally say you got "flak" over a small, quiet complaint from one person. It implies a real storm of disapproval.

b) Flak implies the person has to bear it.
The phrasing is almost always about receiving flak — taking it, catching it, facing it. It suggests a kind of exposure to attack. Just like a pilot has to fly through the flak to complete the mission, a person "taking flak" is often enduring the criticism to stand by their decision.

c) Flak often implies the criticism is somewhat expected or earned.
If someone makes a controversial decision, they can expect flak. The word carries an undertone that the criticism arose from something the person did or said that stirred things up.

d) Flak doesn't always mean the criticism is fair.
Someone can take undeserved flak — being attacked unfairly. The word is neutral on whether the criticism is justified. It simply describes the act of being targeted with hostility, not whether the attackers are right.

• "Catch flak" — to receive criticism ("She caught flak for her comments.")
  • "Take flak" — same as above, often implying endurance ("He took a lot of flak but didn't back down.")
  • "Get flak" — same meaning, slightly more casual
  • "Face flak" — to confront or be met with criticism
  • "Draw flak" — to attract or provoke criticism ("The new policy drew heavy flak from experts.")
  • "Flak jacket" — a protective vest worn by soldiers and journalists in war zones, originally designed to protect against shrapnel (flak). In everyday speech, it's also used as a metaphor for anything that shields you from criticism.
  • "Flak catcher" — an informal term for a person (like a spokesperson or PR representative) whose job is to absorb criticism on behalf of someone more powerful, shielding that person from direct attack.

LiteralBursting anti-aircraft shells and shrapnel that attack aircraft mid-air
FigurativeHarsh criticism or hostile opposition directed at a person or decision

The word always carries the image of being under attack from multiple directions — whether that's a pilot flying through a sky full of exploding shells, or a CEO being bombarded by angry headlines, customer complaints, and public backlash all at once.
6145:
To flake out means to fail to do something you had already agreed or promised to do, usually at the last minute and without a good reason.

When someone "flakes out," they let another person down by not showing up, not following through, or suddenly backing out of a commitment — often without much of an explanation. It signals a lack of reliability.

Think of it this way: Imagine your friend promises to help you move furniture on Saturday. Saturday comes, and instead of showing up, they send you a vague text saying, "Sorry, can't make it." They flaked out on you.

"Flake out" also has a second, separate meaning that is less common but still widely used:

To suddenly fall asleep or collapse from exhaustion.

Example: "She got home after a 14-hour shift and just flaked out on the sofa."

In this sense, it paints the image of someone whose energy completely gives out — they just "fall apart" and crash. You will mostly hear this meaning in casual, everyday speech.
Breaking Down the Two Meanings Side by Side

Meaning 1 — Failing a commitment:

"He said he'd come to the wedding, but he flaked out at the last minute."

→ He didn't show up, even though he had said he would.

Meaning 2 — Collapsing from tiredness:

"The kids played all day and totally flaked out by 7 PM."

→ They fell asleep suddenly because they were exhausted.

The context of the sentence almost always makes it clear which meaning is intended.
Where Does the Word "Flake" Come From?

To understand "flake out," it helps to understand the word "flake" itself.

A flake is a thin, fragile, and lightweight piece of something — like a snowflake or a flake of paint peeling off a wall. These things are:

  • Delicate
  • Unreliable in shape
  • Easily broken or scattered

From this image, the slang term "a flake" developed to describe a person who is similarly fragile and unreliable — someone who "crumbles" when the moment comes to follow through. Over time, this gave birth to the phrasal verb "flake out."

The expression grew popular in American English during the mid-to-late 20th century and has since spread across the English-speaking world.
The Word Family: Flake, Flaky, Flaked Out

Once you learn "flake out," you unlock a whole cluster of related words used in everyday English.

Flake (noun) — A person who habitually cancels plans or fails to follow through.

"Don't count on Derek. He's such a flake."

Flake / Flake on (verb, without "out") — To cancel or not show up.

"She always flakes on our plans."
"He totally flaked on me."

Flaky (adjective) — Used to describe a person or behavior that is unreliable, inconsistent, or hard to count on.

"I like her, but she's a bit flaky — you never know if she'll actually show up."

Flaked out (adjective/past tense) — Describes the state of being fast asleep from exhaustion, OR describes someone who has already backed out of something.

"I found him flaked out on the couch when I got home."
"She flaked out on us again."
Register and Tone: When Is This Phrase Used?

"Flake out" is informal slang. This means:

  • ✅ Use it with friends, family, or in casual conversations.
  • ✅ Use it in text messages or informal writing.
  • ❌ Avoid it in formal settings like job interviews, academic essays, or professional emails.

In formal situations, you would instead say something like:

  • "He failed to honour his commitment."
  • "She cancelled without prior notice."

Yes — in Meaning 1, "flake out" almost always carries a slightly negative or frustrated tone. When you say someone "flaked out," you are implying:

  • They were unreliable.
  • They may have been inconsiderate of your time or effort.
  • Their reason for cancelling was not strong enough to justify it.
