  • Inflection — the fuller form of the word used in both grammar and mathematics. "Flection" in those contexts is essentially a compressed version of "inflection."

If you understand "flection," you automatically have a strong grip on "flexion" and "inflection" as well, because all three are rooted in the same idea of bending.
6174:
When fledgling is used as an adjective, it describes something — or someone — that is new, undeveloped, and still in the early stages of growth or existence.

Think of it this way: something fledgling has only recently come into being. It exists, it has started, but it hasn't yet matured, gained strength, or proven itself fully. It is still finding its footing in the world.

The word carries three layers of meaning at once, and understanding all three is what makes you truly understand it:

1. Newness — The thing has only recently started to exist or operate. It hasn't been around long.

2. Underdevelopment — Because it's so new, it hasn't fully grown. It lacks the stability, experience, or strength that comes with time.

3. Fragility and potential — A fledgling thing is delicate. It could fail. But it also could grow into something strong and established. The word carries both risk and hope at the same time.

This combination is what makes "fledgling" special. It doesn't just mean "new." It means new and still fragile, but with the possibility of growth.
What Kind of Things Can Be "Fledgling"?

The adjective is used broadly. Here are the main categories:

Organizations and institutions:

"A fledgling company" — a business that was started recently and is still struggling to establish itself.
"A fledgling democracy" — a country that has only recently adopted democratic rule and hasn't yet built strong institutions around it.

People and professionals:

"A fledgling actor" — someone who has just entered acting and is still building their skills and reputation.
"A fledgling politician" — someone who is new to politics and still learning how it all works.

Abstract things:

"A fledgling career" — a career that has only just begun.
"A fledgling movement" — a social or political movement that has just started gathering support but hasn't yet become powerful.
"A fledgling industry" — a sector of business that is newly emerging and hasn't yet become large or dominant.

The word feels most at home when describing something with ambition and potential — things that are trying to grow into something bigger.

These examples will show you how the word feels in real use:

  • "The fledgling airline had only three planes and two routes, but it was growing fast."
    The airline is brand new and small, but developing.
  • "As a fledgling writer, she was still learning how to structure her stories."
    She has started writing but is in the early, learning phase of her career.
  • "The peace deal was still fragile — the fledgling ceasefire could collapse at any moment."
    The ceasefire is newly formed and hasn't yet proven its stability.
  • "He invested early in a fledgling tech startup that later became a billion-dollar company."
    The startup was tiny and new at the time, but it grew enormously.

Notice how in every case, the subject exists and has begun, but is not yet mature or established.

"Fledgling" is largely neutral, but it leans toward being slightly sympathetic or hopeful. When you call something fledgling, you are usually not mocking it — you are acknowledging that it is young and growing.

However, it can carry a subtle note of vulnerability or caution. Calling something "a fledgling government" might subtly suggest that it is not yet fully stable and should be watched carefully.

It is almost never used sarcastically or as an insult.
How It Differs From Similar Words

You will come across several words that feel similar. Here is how "fledgling" stands apart:

  • New — Simply means recently created. No sense of fragility or growth. "A new restaurant" just tells you it opened recently. "A fledgling restaurant" tells you it opened recently AND is still finding its way.
  • Budding — Very close to fledgling, but slightly more optimistic. "A budding artist" emphasizes that the person shows promise. "A fledgling artist" emphasizes that the person is simply at an early stage, with the outcome still uncertain.
  • Nascent — Means the same thing but is more formal and academic. You would see "nascent" in academic papers or formal writing; "fledgling" is more common in journalism and everyday writing.
  • Emerging — Focuses on the process of coming into the spotlight. An emerging technology is becoming noticeable to the world. A fledgling technology is simply young and undeveloped — it may not even be noticed yet.

These are common misunderstandings worth clearing up:

  • It does not mean "failed" or "weak." A fledgling thing simply hasn't had time to grow yet. It could become enormously successful.
  • It does not mean "small" by itself — though young things often happen to be small.
  • It does not mean the thing will definitely grow. It just means it's currently at a very early stage.
If you had to remember just one thing: fledgling means newly started and still developing, with a sense that it is fragile but has the potential to grow.
6175:
A fledgling is a young bird that has recently grown its first real feathers and has just left its nest, but is still in the process of learning to fly and survive on its own. It is no longer a helpless, freshly-hatched chick. But it is not yet a fully capable adult bird either. It exists in a precise in-between stage: past the very beginning, but not yet fully formed or ready.

This in-between stage is the heart of the word. A fledgling has developed some real abilities, but it is still fragile, still learning, and still has a long way to go before it truly matures.
The figurative meaning — how people really use it

In everyday language, which is where you will encounter this word most often, "fledgling" is used to describe any person, organization, movement, or system that is newly established and still in its early, developing stages.

Just as a young bird is new, somewhat fragile, and not yet fully capable, a fledgling business is one that has just started out and hasn't yet proven itself or become stable. A fledgling democracy is a newly formed democratic government that is still finding its footing and could still fail. A fledgling artist is someone who has just begun their artistic journey and is still developing their craft.

Here are some examples of the word in sentences:

  • "The fledgling company had only ten employees and was struggling to survive."
  • "Years later, that fledgling democracy became one of the most stable in the region."
  • "She was a fledgling musician, performing in small cafes while she found her voice."
What makes "fledgling" different from simply saying "new"

This distinction is important. When you call something "new," you are simply stating a fact about time — it hasn't existed for very long. When you call something a "fledgling," you are communicating something much richer and more specific.

You are saying it is new, yes — but beyond that, you are also saying it is still actively developing and has not yet reached maturity. You are saying it is somewhat fragile or uncertain, and could still fail or falter. And yet, crucially, you are not dismissing it — the word quietly acknowledges that this thing carries potential. It could grow into something much bigger and stronger.

"Fledgling" is therefore a word packed with a quiet tension: it holds vulnerability and hope at the same time. "New" is a plain, flat fact. "Fledgling" is a judgment about a stage of growth — where something stands on the long road from nothing to fully formed.

"Fledgling" has a slightly tender, careful tone. When a writer or speaker uses it, they are not mocking or dismissing the thing they are describing. They are being honest about its current limitations while also respecting its potential. It is a realistic word, but not a harsh one.

Depending on the context, it can also carry a gentle note of caution. To call something a fledgling is to quietly remind the listener: don't expect too much from it yet. It hasn't fully proven itself. It still needs time and the right conditions to grow.
Where you will commonly encounter this word

You'll come across "fledgling" most often in journalism, non-fiction, and serious writing. Writers and reporters use it to describe new companies, new political systems, new careers, new artistic movements, and new international agreements. It signals: "This is something real and worth paying attention to — but it is still in its early stages, and its future is not yet guaranteed."
A mental image to lock the word in your memory

Whenever you see or hear "fledgling," picture a small bird perched nervously on the edge of a branch, wings half-spread, preparing for one of its first real flights. It has the feathers. It has the wings. It has survived long enough to get here. But it hasn't proven itself yet. It is young, it is trying, it is full of potential — and it is not quite there yet.

That image is the soul of the word "fledgling," whether it is describing a bird, a business, a nation, or a human being just starting out on a long journey.
6176:
To flee means to run away from someone or something — quickly and urgently — because of fear, danger, or threat. It is not ordinary leaving. When someone flees, they are driven by a powerful force pushing them away: they have to get away, and they get away fast.

Think of it this way: you don't flee a boring party. You flee a burning building.

The word "flee" carries two built-in ideas at the same time:

  1. Movement away from something (leaving, running, escaping)
  2. A reason for that movement — usually fear, danger, threat, or something deeply unpleasant

This is what separates "flee" from simply "leave" or "go away." When someone leaves a place, it's neutral — no particular feeling is attached. But when someone flees, there is always a story of urgency and distress behind it.

You can flee from something, or you can flee something directly. Both are correct.

  • He fled from the angry crowd.
  • He fled the angry crowd.

The thing being fled is almost always a source of danger, harm, or fear — a person, a place, a situation, or even an idea.

FormWord
Base formflee
Past tensefled
Past participlefled
Present participlefleeing

The most important thing to remember is the irregular past tense: fled (not "fleed"). This is one of the most common mistakes learners make.

  • Thousands of people fled the city after the earthquake.
  • The suspect fled before police arrived.
  • People are fleeing the conflict zone.

1. War and conflict
People forced out of their homes by war, violence, or persecution are said to flee. This is why you'll often read about refugees fleeing war zones or people fleeing persecution.

Millions of civilians had to flee their homes as the fighting intensified.

2. Natural disasters
When a hurricane, wildfire, flood, or earthquake strikes, people flee the affected area.

Residents were forced to flee as the wildfire moved toward the town.

3. Crime and law enforcement
A criminal running from police is said to flee.

The robber fled on foot after the alarm went off.

4. Animals
Animals running from predators or danger also flee.

The deer fled into the forest when it heard the gunshot.
An Important Distinction: Flee vs. Escape

These two words are close in meaning but not identical.

  • Flee describes the urgent act of running away. It focuses on the motion away from danger. You can flee and still be caught.
  • Escape focuses on the successful outcome — getting away safely. When you escape, you make it out.

So: you flee a burning building, and you escape the fire. You can flee from the police but be caught before you escape.

In many situations, both words can be used — but "flee" puts the spotlight on the fear-driven running, while "escape" puts the spotlight on successfully getting free.

Both mean leaving quickly out of fear, but there's a subtle tonal difference:

  • Run away is more everyday and informal. A child might run away from a spider.
  • Flee is more serious and formal. It is used for genuine danger — war, disaster, violence, persecution. It carries more weight and gravity.

The child ran away from the dog. ✓ (everyday, light)
The child fled the burning house. ✓ (serious, urgent)

You could say "the child fled from the dog," and it would be grammatically correct — but it might sound slightly dramatic for such a small event. "Flee" naturally fits high-stakes situations.

"Flee" doesn't always mean physically running. It can be used figuratively — to describe emotionally or mentally withdrawing from something uncomfortable.

He fled from responsibility his entire life. (He avoided it, ran from it emotionally.)
She fled into sleep to escape her worries. (She used sleep as a mental escape.)

In these cases, there is no physical running — but the same sense of urgency and escape applies, just on an emotional or psychological level.

QuestionAnswer
What does it mean?To run away quickly due to fear or danger
Is it neutral?No — it always implies urgency and a threatening reason
What's irregular?Past tense is fled, not "fleed"
Is it formal or informal?Formal/serious — used for real danger, not small everyday situations
Can it be figurative?Yes — fleeing responsibility, fleeing one's past, etc.
Three Sentences That Show the Full Spectrum

1. (Literal, physical danger): The family fled their country to escape the civil war.
  2. (Criminal context): The suspect fled the scene before authorities arrived.
  3. (Figurative): For years, he had been fleeing the painful memories of his childhood.

That is everything you need to know about "flee." The heart of the word is this: urgent movement, driven by fear, away from danger — whether that danger is a wildfire, a war, a predator, or even one's own past.
6177:
A fleece is the full coat of wool that naturally grows on a sheep's body. Think of it as the sheep's built-in "sweater" — a thick, dense, soft layer of woolly fibers covering almost the entire animal. This coat grows continuously throughout the year, keeping the sheep warm in cold weather.

Other woolly animals — such as alpacas, llamas, and certain goats like Angora goats — also grow a fleece. So while sheep are the most classic example, the word applies to any animal with a comparable woolly coat.
The Shorn Fleece: Wool Removed from the Animal

Once or twice a year, farmers shear (cut) this wool off the sheep. When done skillfully, the entire coat comes off in one large, connected piece — almost like peeling a sweater off the animal in a single sheet. That removed piece is also called a fleece.

So the word covers two closely related things:

  • The wool coat on the living animal
  • The same wool coat after it has been cut off and removed

Both are called a fleece. The distinction only matters when context requires it — for example, a farmer might say "we sheared ten fleeces today," meaning they removed ten full wool coats from ten sheep.

In everyday modern life, this is perhaps the most common way you'll hear the word used. Fleece now refers to a popular type of soft, warm, lightweight fabric — the kind used in cozy jackets, pullovers, hoodies, blankets, and winter accessories.

This fabric is almost always made from synthetic materials (typically polyester), not from actual sheep's wool. It's called fleece simply because it mimics the feel of natural wool — it's fuzzy, warm, and comfortable against the skin. It also has another wool-like quality: it traps body heat effectively while remaining breathable.

You've almost certainly owned or touched something made of this material — those warm, slightly fuzzy-surfaced winter jackets or soft blankets are classic examples of fleece fabric.

Because of the fabric above, "a fleece" has also become a common word for a jacket or top made from fleece fabric. This usage is very natural in everyday British and American English.

For example: "It's cold outside — I'll grab my fleece." Here, "fleece" simply means a warm, soft pullover or zip-up jacket made from the fabric described above.

So depending on context, "a fleece" might refer to the item of clothing, not the raw material.

You may also encounter the phrase fleece-lined, which describes a garment or product that has a layer of fleece on the inside for extra warmth and softness — for example, fleece-lined boots, gloves, or trousers. The outside might be a different material entirely, but the inner lining is fleece.
The Golden Fleece: A Famous Cultural Reference

You will likely come across the phrase the Golden Fleece at some point in literature, history, or popular culture. This comes from an ancient Greek myth. It refers to the magical, shimmering fleece of a divine golden ram — a legendary treasure of immense value and power.

In the myth, a hero named Jason, along with his crew called the Argonauts, embarks on a dangerous sea quest to find and retrieve this Golden Fleece. The phrase has since come to symbolize any precious, difficult-to-obtain prize worth great sacrifice. It still appears in book titles, company names, and literary references today.

In older or literary writing, you may occasionally see "fleece" used to describe soft, white, wispy patches of cloud that resemble tufts of wool — as in "fleeces of cloud drifted across the sky." This is a poetic metaphor, not a standard everyday meaning. If you encounter it, you'll recognize it immediately from the visual image it creates.

Connecting all of these meanings is a single core idea: something soft, warm, and wooly — either literally (the animal's coat, the fabric, the garment) or figuratively (the cloud image, the mythological treasure). Once you understand that thread, every use of the word will feel natural and intuitive.
6178:
To fleece someone means to cheat them out of their money — usually a lot of it — through dishonesty, trickery, or by charging an outrageously unfair price. The person being fleeced doesn't realize what's happening, or realizes it only when it's too late.

Think of it this way: someone tricks you into trusting them, and then uses that trust to drain your wallet. That's fleecing.
What Makes It Different From Just "Stealing"

This is important. Fleecing is not the same as a pickpocket stealing your wallet or a burglar breaking into your house. The key difference is:

  • In regular theft, something is taken from you by force or secretly, without any interaction.
  • When you are fleeced, there is a transaction involved — you are made to willingly hand over your money, but only because you have been deceived, misled, or taken advantage of. You think you're getting something fair. You're not.

The dishonesty is baked right into the word. You can't fleece someone honestly. The moment it's fair, it's no longer fleecing.

"Fleece" carries a strong sense of being completely stripped of your money — not just a little overcharged, but significantly robbed through cunning. It suggests the person doing it is deliberately and coldly exploiting someone who is trusting, naive, or simply unaware.

It is also a slightly informal word. You'd use it in everyday conversation, not in a legal document (a lawyer would use words like "defraud"). But it's not slang — it's a proper, widely understood English word.

The person doing the fleecing is almost always in a position of informational advantage — they know something the victim doesn't, and they exploit that gap. Common fleecer-and-victim relationships:

  • A dishonest mechanic and a car owner who knows nothing about engines
  • A scammer or con artist and a trusting elderly person
  • A corrupt vendor and a tourist unfamiliar with local prices
  • A shady financial advisor and someone who blindly trusts them with savings
  • A company using hidden fees and customers who don't read the fine print

The victim is almost always trusting, vulnerable, inexperienced, or simply distracted.

Pretty serious. Fleecing isn't a minor rip-off. If a coffee shop charges you $3.50 instead of $3, nobody would say you were fleeced. But if a mechanic charges you $3,000 for a $200 repair and invents fake problems to justify it — that's fleecing. The word implies a significant and deliberate swindle, not a small inconvenience.
Grammar: How to Use It in a Sentence

The structure is simple: someone fleeces someone (else).

  • Subject (the cheater) + fleeced + object (the victim)

You can also add what they were fleeced out of:

  • Subject + fleeced + object + out of + (money/amount)

These examples will show you the full range of how the word is used in real life:

  1. "The mechanic fleeced me. He charged $2,500 for a problem that didn't even exist."

(A dishonest professional exploiting a customer's ignorance.)

  1. "Tourists in that area are routinely fleeced by taxi drivers who take unnecessarily long routes and charge triple the normal fare."

(A common victim: someone unfamiliar with local norms.)

  1. "That investment scheme fleeced hundreds of retirees out of their life savings."

(Large-scale, deliberate financial fraud.)

  1. "I felt completely fleeced after I realized the 'luxury hotel' I booked online looked nothing like the photos."

(Deceptive marketing leading to a feeling of being cheated.)

  1. "Don't buy electronics at that market — they'll fleece you if you don't know the local prices."

(A warning to someone who lacks information the sellers have.)

  1. "He posed as a financial advisor and fleeced his clients for years before anyone noticed."

(A con artist using a false identity to gain trust and then exploit it.)

Knowing nearby words helps you understand a word more deeply.

  • Swindle — very close in meaning; slightly more formal. Emphasizes the clever scheme.
  • Con — short for "confidence trick." Focuses on building false trust first.
  • Defraud — the formal/legal version. Used in courts and official documents.
  • Rip off — more casual and broader; can apply to smaller, everyday overcharging.
  • Scam — focuses on the scheme or trick used, not just the victim's loss.
  • Cheat — the most general of these; fleecing is a specific, more severe kind of cheating.

Fleece sits comfortably in the middle — more vivid and punchy than "defraud," more serious than "rip off," and strongly implying a substantial financial loss through deliberate dishonesty.

To sharpen your understanding, here's what the word does not cover:

  • ❌ An honest business charging high prices (that's just expensive, not fleecing)
  • ❌ A friend borrowing money and forgetting to pay back (careless, not deliberate deception)
  • ❌ A straightforward robbery or theft (fleecing always involves a transaction or interaction)
  • ❌ A small, accidental overcharge (fleecing is intentional and usually significant)
One-Line Summary to Remember It Forever

To fleece someone = to deliberately cheat them, usually out of a significant amount of money, by taking advantage of their trust or ignorance — making them hand it over willingly, without realizing they're being robbed.
6179: To fleer means to mock or laugh at someone with open contempt and scorn. It's not a gentle tease or a friendly joke — it's a sharp, sneering kind of mockery that is meant to make the other person feel small, foolish, or inferior.

The word carries two things at once: contempt (a feeling that someone is beneath you or worthless) and expression (showing that contempt openly, often through your face and laughter).

When someone fleers, they don't just think badly of you in their head — they show it. Think of a person curling their lip, grinning with mockery, or laughing in someone's face in a way that drips with disrespect. That is fleering.

So the word sits right at the intersection of sneering and laughing at — it's what happens when scorn wears a grin.

This is important: fleering often has a visible, physical quality to it. It's not just mockery in words. It tends to involve:

  • A contemptuous smirk or sneer on the face
  • A mocking laugh or grin directed at someone
  • An open, bold display of disrespect — the person doing it isn't hiding how little they think of you

Imagine a court jester sneering behind a king's back, or a group of students laughing openly at a classmate who stumbles. That visible, sneering laughter is the soul of "fleer."

Fleering is cold and cruel, not playful. It comes from a place of feeling superior. The person who fleers is essentially saying, "Look at you. You're ridiculous. You're beneath me." — not with words necessarily, but with their expression and laughter.

It is different from:

  • Teasing — which can be affectionate
  • Joking — which is usually light-hearted
  • Laughing with someone — which is shared joy

Fleering is always laughing at someone, never with them.
How It Compares to Similar Words

Understanding "fleer" becomes much sharper when you place it next to words it resembles:

Fleer vs. Mock: To mock is the broader act of making fun of someone. Fleering is a specific kind of mocking — one expressed through a visible sneer or contemptuous laugh. All fleering is mocking, but not all mocking is fleering.

Fleer vs. Sneer: A sneer is an expression of contempt, usually through the face or voice. Fleering adds the element of laughter and open ridicule to that contempt. A sneer can be silent; a fleer is more active and derisive.

Fleer vs. Jeer: To jeer is to shout or call out mockingly, often in a crowd (think of an audience jeering at a performer). Fleering can be more personal and intimate — a quiet, cold, contemptuous smirk directed at one person, not a loud crowd reaction.

Fleer vs. Taunt: To taunt is to provoke someone with words, often to get a reaction. Fleering is less about provocation and more about expressing contempt and ridicule — sometimes without a single word.

Fleer vs. Scoff: To scoff is to dismiss something as stupid or unworthy (you scoff at an idea). Fleering is more personal — you fleer at a person, targeting them with contemptuous laughter.

These examples will help you see the word alive:

  • "The older boys fleered at his handmade shoes, nudging each other and grinning."

Here, the mockery is visible and social — aimed at making him feel ashamed.

  • "She tried to read her poem aloud, but half the audience simply fleered."

The audience responded not with thoughtful criticism but with open, contemptuous laughter.

  • "He fleered at every suggestion she made, as if she were too foolish to be taken seriously."

This shows the "superiority" element — he treats her ideas as laughably beneath him.

  • "The villain fleered at the hero's sense of justice, smirking as though it were the funniest thing he'd ever heard."

A classic literary use — contemptuous mockery directed at something the villain considers naive.

"Fleer" is a literary and somewhat archaic word. You are far more likely to encounter it in classic literature, Shakespeare, poetry, or formal writing than in everyday conversation. It appears in Shakespeare's plays, for example, where characters fleer at one another in moments of contempt.

In modern speech, people rarely say "fleer" — they'd more likely say sneer at, mock, or laugh at. But the word is precise and powerful, and once you know it, you'll spot it immediately in older texts.

To fleer = to openly mock someone with contemptuous, sneering laughter — expressing scorn through your face and attitude, making clear that you find them laughably inferior.

That's the word, completely. Every time you see it, ask yourself: Is someone showing contemptuous, sneering mockery toward another person? If yes — that's fleering.
6180:
A fleet is a group of vehicles — especially ships, but also aircraft, cars, or trucks — that belong to the same owner or organization and are used together for a shared purpose.

The single most important thing to understand about the word is this: a fleet is not just any random collection of vehicles sitting near each other. It's a group that is owned, operated, or commanded as a unit — like a team, but made of vehicles.
The Original and Primary Meaning — Ships

The word is most strongly associated with ships. When you hear "fleet" without any other context, most people picture ships on the sea.

A naval fleet is a group of warships that operate together under one military command. Countries build and maintain fleets to project power across the seas, protect their waters, or fight wars. For example, "the enemy fleet was spotted on the horizon" means a group of enemy warships moving together.

The entire naval fighting force of a country can also be called its fleet. So you might say "the country's fleet was the most powerful in the world," meaning all the warships that country owns and commands.

A fleet doesn't have to be military, though. A shipping company that owns many cargo vessels also has a fleet. If a company owns 40 large ships that carry goods across the ocean, those 40 ships together are their fleet.
The Idea Extends to Other Vehicles

Over time, the word expanded naturally from ships to other kinds of vehicles. The logic is exactly the same: a group of vehicles, under one ownership or command, used together.

Aircraft: An airline's fleet is all the planes it owns and operates. When an airline says "our fleet includes 200 aircraft," it means it owns and flies 200 planes. The military equivalent is an air fleet — a large formation of warplanes operating under unified command.

Cars and trucks: A company that owns many vehicles for its business operations has a fleet of vehicles. A delivery company might have a fleet of 500 vans. A taxi company has a fleet of cabs. A large corporation might give company cars to its employees — those cars together are called the corporate fleet.

Buses: A city's public transport authority operates a fleet of buses. All the buses running in a city under one transit authority are that authority's fleet.

No matter which type of vehicle you're talking about, the word "fleet" always carries these two essential qualities:

  1. Plurality — There is more than one vehicle. You cannot have a fleet of one ship. A fleet is always a group.
  2. Unity of ownership or command — The vehicles belong to the same entity (a government, a company, a military force) or operate under the same authority. This is what separates a fleet from just "a bunch of ships in the same ocean." Random ships from different countries passing each other are not a fleet. The same ships, all owned by one navy and sailing together under one admiral, are a fleet.

The word doesn't specify an exact number, but it generally implies a significant, organized group — not just two or three.

In military contexts, a fleet is typically a very large force — dozens to hundreds of warships. It is the largest operational unit of a navy. In many navies, a fleet is subdivided into smaller groups called squadrons or flotillas.

In commercial and everyday contexts, the bar is lower. A company with just 10 delivery vans might still call them "our fleet." The key is still unity of ownership, not sheer size. However, if a small business owner has two work trucks, they would be unlikely to call those a fleet — the word carries a connotation of scale and organization.

You'll often encounter the word in business and logistics.

  • Fleet management is the job of overseeing and maintaining a company's vehicles — keeping them serviced, tracking them, replacing old ones.
  • A fleet vehicle is a car or truck owned by a company rather than a private individual. Rental car companies, for instance, buy vehicles in bulk for their fleets.
  • Fleet size is how many vehicles an organization owns. "The airline grew its fleet to 300 planes" means it now owns 300 aircraft.
Quick Examples to Cement the Idea

• "The admiral commanded a fleet of 30 warships." — A naval fleet under military command.
  • "The fishing company had a fleet of trawlers operating in the North Sea." — Commercial ships under one company.
  • "The airline retired several older planes from its fleet." — All the aircraft an airline operates.
  • "The city's entire fleet of garbage trucks went on strike." — All the trucks owned by the city's waste department.
  • "Our sales team drives fleet cars provided by the company." — Vehicles owned by a company for employee use.

A fleet is a group of vehicles — originally and most commonly ships, but also aircraft, cars, or trucks — that are owned by the same organization or operating under the same command, functioning together as a coordinated unit.
6181:
Something fleeting lasts for only a very short time and disappears quickly — so quickly, in fact, that you can barely hold onto it before it's gone.

Think of a soap bubble. The moment it appears, it's already on its way to vanishing. That is the spirit of fleeting. It doesn't just mean short. It means passing so fast that it almost slips past you entirely.

This is what makes fleeting special. It's not a cold, clinical word for "short duration." It carries a gentle emotional weight — often a sense of wistfulness, a quiet sadness that something beautiful or pleasant didn't stay long enough. When you call something fleeting, you're not just describing time. You're expressing that the shortness mattered. It felt brief.

Here are natural sentences to show how the word works in real life:

  • "I caught a fleeting glimpse of the deer before it disappeared into the forest." — You saw it for barely a second.
  • "She gave me a fleeting smile and walked away." — The smile appeared and vanished in an instant.
  • "Happiness can be fleeting if you don't learn to appreciate the small moments." — Happiness doesn't always stay; it passes.
  • "A fleeting thought crossed his mind, but he forgot it before he could write it down." — The thought was there and gone in a flash.
  • "Youth is fleeting — enjoy it while it lasts." — Youth doesn't last; it passes faster than we realize.
  • "There was a fleeting moment of silence before the crowd erupted." — The silence lasted only a second or two.
How It Differs from Similar Words

Several words are close in meaning to fleeting, but each has its own shade:

Brief simply means short in duration. It's neutral and factual. "The meeting was brief." No emotion attached.

Momentary means lasting only a moment — roughly one instant. "A momentary lapse in concentration." It's about a single, tiny unit of time.

Fleeting goes a step further than both. It suggests something is moving, passing through — like it's in a hurry to leave. It has motion built into it. Something fleeting doesn't just end quickly; it slips away.

Transient and ephemeral are close cousins too, but they're more formal and often used in philosophical or literary writing. Fleeting is more natural in everyday speech and writing.

Certain words appear with fleeting very naturally. Getting familiar with these combinations will help you use the word confidently:

  • A fleeting moment — a moment that passes too fast
  • A fleeting glance — a very quick look
  • A fleeting thought — an idea that crosses your mind and disappears before you can fully form it
  • A fleeting feeling — an emotion that comes and goes quickly
  • A fleeting visit — a very short stay
  • A fleeting impression — a quick, passing sense of something
  • Fleeting beauty — beauty that doesn't last
  • Fleeting fame — fame that disappears quickly

It helps to be clear about what the word does not mean:

  • It does not mean "unimportant." A fleeting moment can be incredibly significant — a fleeting look between two people can change a relationship forever.
  • It does not mean "fake" or "unreal." The thing is absolutely real — it's just brief.
  • It does not describe something that might be short. It describes something that is brief, whether you're observing it or reflecting on it.

Knowing the opposites sharpens your understanding:

  • Lasting — something that endures over a long time
  • Permanent — something that doesn't go away
  • Enduring — something that survives the test of time
  • Eternal — something that never ends

So if a fleeting love is one that fades fast, an enduring love is one that stands the test of time.

Fleeting is a word about the relationship between time and loss. Humans use it most often when talking about things that are precious because they don't last — beauty, youth, joy, a perfect moment. In that way, the word isn't just a description. It's a small, quiet acknowledgment that some of the best things in life pass before we're ready to let them go.

That's the full picture of fleeting — a word small in size but rich in meaning.
6182: "Flesh and blood" is an idiom with three closely related but distinct meanings. All three meanings are rooted in the same big idea: that human beings are physical, mortal creatures — not robots, not gods — and that they come in families.
Meaning 1: A Close Family Member (by birth)

This is the most common and emotionally powerful use of the phrase.

When you call someone "your own flesh and blood," you mean they are your biological relative — your child, parent, sibling, or another blood relation. It emphasizes that you share the same blood, the same biological origins. The phrase carries a deep emotional weight — it implies a bond that is natural, permanent, and almost sacred.

Example sentences:

  • "How could he turn his back on his own flesh and blood?" — This means: how could he abandon his own family?
  • "She raised that child as her own flesh and blood." — She treated the child exactly like a biological family member.
  • "No matter what my brother does, I will always stand by him. He is my flesh and blood."

The feeling behind this meaning: When people use this phrase about family, they're usually expressing that family ties come with a special kind of loyalty or obligation. There's an unspoken rule in many cultures: you don't abandon your flesh and blood. The idiom makes that emotional argument very powerfully.
Meaning 2: A Real, Living Human Being

The second meaning is used to remind someone (or yourself) that a person is just a human — not a machine, not a superhero, not a god. Real humans get tired. They make mistakes. They feel pain, emotions, and fear. They have limits.

You'll often hear this in the phrase "only flesh and blood."

Example sentences:

  • "Stop expecting her to work 18-hour days without a break. She's only flesh and blood!" — She's just a human being with a human body; she needs rest.
  • "Even the greatest athletes are flesh and blood — they get injuries just like anyone else."
  • "He may seem fearless, but he's flesh and blood like the rest of us."

The feeling behind this meaning: There's often a sense of empathy or defense here. When someone says "he's only flesh and blood," they're usually defending a person against unrealistic expectations. It's a way of humanizing someone.
Meaning 3: The Limits of What a Person Can Endure

This meaning is an extension of Meaning 2. It's used to say that something is too painful, difficult, or distressing for any human to tolerate. Every person has a breaking point, and this phrase highlights that.

You'll often hear it in the pattern: "more than flesh and blood can bear/stand/endure."

Example sentences:

  • "Watching her child suffer day after day — it was more than flesh and blood could bear." — No human being could endure that emotional pain.
  • "The heat in the factory was more than flesh and blood could stand; the workers had to stop."
  • "Years of injustice, and still no help. It was more than flesh and blood could endure."

The feeling behind this meaning: This usage is deeply empathetic. It validates that what a person is going through is genuinely, objectively intolerable — not a sign of weakness, but proof of being human.
Where Did This Idiom Come From?

The phrase is ancient. It has been found in the English language for over 600 years and is one of the oldest surviving idioms in English.

Its most famous early source is the Bible. In the King James Version (published in 1611), the phrase appears multiple times. One well-known example is from Ephesians 6:12, which speaks of a struggle "not against flesh and blood" — meaning not against ordinary human beings. Another is from Matthew 16:17, where Jesus tells Peter that his knowledge did not come from flesh and blood — meaning not from any human source.

Because the Bible was read by almost everyone in English-speaking societies for centuries, phrases from it entered everyday language and stuck. "Flesh and blood" is one of them.

Before the Bible became widespread in English, the phrase was already being used by writers in the 14th and 15th centuries. It was simply the most natural way to describe the physical reality of a human body: flesh (the soft tissue) and blood (the liquid of life). Together, they represented the whole living human being.

This is a formal-to-neutral idiom. It is not slang. It is not casual in the way that street expressions are. You can use it in:

  • Everyday conversation — "She's my own flesh and blood; I'll help her no matter what."
  • Writing — novels, essays, speeches.
  • Emotional moments — arguments, reconciliations, expressions of loyalty.

It is rarely used in professional/business contexts, unless the topic is deeply human (like a speech about family, sacrifice, or human dignity).
The Full Range of Example Sentences (Summary)

Here are examples covering all three meanings in realistic contexts:

Family meaning:

  • "I don't care what people say about my son. He's my flesh and blood, and I'll defend him."
  • "It broke her heart to see her flesh and blood struggling with poverty."

Being human meaning:

  • "Don't treat him like a machine — he's flesh and blood, just like you."
  • "Even the toughest soldiers are flesh and blood. They need sleep and food."

Human limits meaning:

  • "Watching that tragedy unfold without being able to help — it was more than flesh and blood could stand."
  • "Years of sleepless nights caring for her family — it was more than flesh and blood could endure."

• "My own flesh and blood" — the most emotional, most personal version; used for family.
  • "Only flesh and blood" — used to remind that someone is merely human.
  • "More than flesh and blood can bear/stand/endure" — used to describe intolerable pain or suffering.
  • "Flesh and blood cannot..." — used to express something beyond human capability or tolerance.
What NOT to Confuse It With

"Flesh and blood" ≠ "blood and guts."
"Blood and guts" refers to graphic violence or raw, tough content. They sound similar but mean very different things.

"Flesh and blood" ≠ "in cold blood."
"In cold blood" means to do something (usually violent) in a deliberate, emotionless way. Completely different idiom.

"Flesh and blood" ≠ literally talking about the body.
If a doctor says "the flesh and blood show signs of infection," that is literal medical language. The idiom is always about humanness, family, or human limits — not clinical descriptions of the body.

Think of it this way: "Flesh and blood" = being human.

And being human means three things this idiom captures perfectly:

  1. You belong to a family.
  2. You are not a machine or a god.
  3. You can only take so much.

Every time you see or hear this phrase, ask yourself which of those three ideas is being expressed, and you'll understand it perfectly every time.
6183:
To flesh out means to add more detail, depth, and substance to something so that it becomes fuller and more complete.

Think of it this way: imagine you have just a stick figure drawing. It shows the basic shape of a person, but nothing more. Now imagine you start drawing in the muscles, the skin, the curves, and the features. You are turning a bare skeleton into a full, complete body. That process — going from a bare outline to something rich and complete — is exactly what "flesh out" means.

When someone says "flesh out your idea," they're saying: "Right now your idea is just a skeleton. Put some flesh on it. Give it life and detail."

The phrase is rooted in a very literal image from the human body. "Flesh" refers to the soft tissue — the muscles and skin — that covers a skeleton. A skeleton alone gives you the basic structure, but it has no substance, no richness. It needs flesh to become something real and complete.

This idea was borrowed into the English language as a metaphor. Skeletons became outlines, ideas, plans, or rough drafts. Flesh became details, explanation, and depth. So "fleshing out" something means building it up from a bare-bones version into a complete, well-developed one.

Here are clear examples showing how the phrase is used in real life:

  • "Can you flesh out your proposal a little more before the meeting?"

(Your proposal exists, but it's too brief. Add more details to make it stronger.)

  • "The novelist needed to flesh out her characters."

(The characters felt flat and underdeveloped. She needed to give them more personality, history, and depth.)

  • "We have the basic concept for the app, but we need to flesh it out."

(The concept is there, but it's incomplete. More thought and detail are needed.)

  • "The teacher asked him to flesh out his answer."

(His answer was too short and vague. She wanted him to explain more fully.)

  • "The plan was fleshed out over several meetings."

(The plan started rough and incomplete, but gradually became detailed and thorough through discussion.)

"Flesh out" is a phrasal verb, meaning it's a verb made up of two words that work together as a single unit.

Here are the different grammatical forms:

  • Base form: flesh out — "I need to flesh out this idea."
  • Past tense: fleshed out — "She fleshed out the argument with strong evidence."
  • Present participle: fleshing out — "He is currently fleshing out the details."
  • As an adjective: well-fleshed-out — "This is a well-fleshed-out plan."

Important grammar note about pronouns: When you replace the object with a pronoun (like it or them), the pronoun goes between the two words — not after "out."

✅ Correct: "Let me flesh it out."
❌ Incorrect: "Let me flesh out it."

But when the object is a full noun phrase, it can go either way:
✅ "Let me flesh out the plan."
✅ "Let me flesh the plan out."
Both are correct.

"Flesh out" doesn't just mean adding more words. It specifically means adding meaningful, relevant substance. The additions should genuinely improve the quality and completeness of something — not just make it longer for the sake of length.

For example:

  • Adding more evidence to support a claim ✅
  • Adding more explanation to a confusing section ✅
  • Adding more background to a character ✅
  • Just repeating the same point in different words ❌ (This isn't fleshing out — this is padding.)

This is an important distinction. "Flesh out" carries a positive connotation. It implies real enrichment.

"Flesh out" appears across many different areas of life:

  • Writing: An author fleshes out a character by giving them a backstory, personality quirks, and clear motivations.
  • Business: A team fleshes out a business plan by adding financial projections, timelines, and specific goals.
  • Academic work: A student fleshes out an essay by supporting arguments with evidence and examples.
  • Design/Product development: A designer fleshes out a rough concept by working through the specific features and details.
  • Conversations: You flesh out an explanation when someone says they're confused and you give them more detail.
The Big Confusion: "Flesh Out" vs. "Flush Out"

This is one of the most common mistakes in the English language, so it deserves special attention.

"Flesh out" and "flush out" sound similar, but they mean completely different things.

"Flush out" means to force something or someone out of a hiding place, or to clean something by pushing liquid through it.

  • "The detective managed to flush out the suspect from his hideout."

(He forced the suspect to come out of hiding.)

  • "Flush out the pipe with water."

(Clean the pipe by running water through it to push the dirt out.)

"Flesh out" means to add detail and substance.

  • "The detective fleshed out his theory with new evidence."

(He added more detail and support to his theory.)

A very common mistake is saying "flush out an idea" when the person actually means "flesh out an idea." You flesh out ideas — you make them more complete. You flush out things that are hiding — you bring them into the open. Remember: flesh = adding substance; flush = forcing something out.

These words are related to "flesh out," but each has a slightly different feel:

  • Elaborate on — similar, but more often used when speaking. ("Can you elaborate on that point?")
  • Expand on — means to make something longer and broader in scope.
  • Develop — more general; can mean to improve over time, not just by adding detail.
  • Round out — means to complete something by filling in what's missing, making it balanced.
  • Fill in the details — very direct and informal; means the same thing.
  • Build out — common in business and tech; means to develop something further from a starting point.

"Flesh out" is slightly more vivid and specific than all of these because of its imagery of giving life and body to something bare.

What it meansTo add detail, depth, and substance to something incomplete
Where it comes fromThe image of adding flesh (muscle/skin) to a bare skeleton
TonePositive — it implies genuine improvement
Common confusionDon't mix it up with "flush out," which means to force something out of hiding
Key formsflesh out / fleshed out / fleshing out / well-fleshed-out

After reading this, you know not just what the phrase means, but why it means that, how to use it correctly in grammar, where it appears in real life, and how to avoid the most common mistake people make with it. You've got the full picture — the skeleton is completely fleshed out.
6184:
To understand "fleshly," start with the word it comes from: flesh — the soft physical material of the human body. When something is described as "fleshly," it means it belongs to, comes from, or concerns the physical body — as opposed to the mind, soul, or spirit.

Think of humans as having two sides: a physical side (the body, with its hungers, desires, and sensations) and a spiritual/mental side (the soul, conscience, or intellect). "Fleshly" always puts something firmly on the physical body side of that divide.

"Fleshly" carries a few closely related meanings depending on how it's used.

Sense 1: Relating to the body in a basic, physical way

At its most straightforward, "fleshly" simply means of or relating to the physical body, the way "bodily" does.

"Fleshly needs" — the body's basic needs: food, warmth, rest, comfort.
"Fleshly existence" — life as a physical, mortal being.

Here the word is fairly neutral. It's just pointing to the fact that something belongs to the realm of the body, not the mind or spirit.

Sense 2: Relating to bodily desires and sensual pleasures

This is the most common and most important sense. "Fleshly" very often refers specifically to the desires and appetites of the body — not just the need for food or rest, but especially sexual desire, pleasure-seeking, and physical gratification.

"Fleshly desires" — the body's cravings and urges, especially sexual ones.
"Fleshly pleasures" — enjoyments that are purely physical and sensory in nature.
"Fleshly lusts" — strong bodily appetites that pull a person toward physical indulgence.

This sense almost always carries a moral overtone — particularly in religious and philosophical writing. The "flesh" is seen as the lower, animal part of human nature that pulls people away from virtue, self-discipline, or God. So "fleshly" in this sense is not just descriptive — it subtly suggests something excessive, tempting, or spiritually dangerous.

Think of it this way: when someone calls a desire "fleshly," they're usually implying that the desire is real and powerful, but that giving in to it entirely is unwise, undignified, or spiritually harmful.

Sense 3: Worldly or earthly (as opposed to spiritual or divine)

In religious and philosophical contexts, "fleshly" broadens out to mean belonging to the earthly, material world — in contrast to anything divine, holy, or spiritually elevated.

"Fleshly wisdom" — cleverness or intelligence that is purely human and worldly, not inspired by God or higher principles.
"Fleshly minded" — preoccupied with the things of this world (money, comfort, pleasure, power) rather than spiritual matters.
"Fleshly reasoning" — conclusions arrived at through purely human logic, without spiritual insight.

In this sense, "fleshly" is almost synonymous with "worldly" — and it carries the same implicit criticism: that something focused entirely on earthly things is missing a higher, more important dimension.

Sense 4: Physically resembling flesh (rare, literary)

Occasionally — and less commonly — "fleshly" is used in a purely descriptive, sensory way to mean having the look, feel, or quality of flesh: soft, warm, physical, tangible.

"Fleshly lips" — lips described in a way that emphasises their physical, bodily reality.
"Fleshly form" — a body described in its warm, tangible, physical presence.

This sense is mostly found in poetry or very literary writing, and it simply highlights the physical realness of something.

No matter which sense is being used, "fleshly" always implies a contrast between the body and something higher — the spirit, the soul, the divine, or the intellectual. The word places something on the side of the physical, mortal, and earthly. Whether that's neutral, slightly negative, or very negative depends on the context — but the contrast is almost always there, at least in the background.

"Fleshly" is not a casual, everyday word. You won't typically hear it in ordinary conversation. It belongs to a more formal, literary, philosophical, or religious register. You are most likely to encounter it in:

  • The Bible and religious texts ("fleshly lusts," "fleshly minded")
  • Older English literature (Shakespeare's era and beyond)
  • Philosophy or moral writing
  • Poetry that deals with the body, desire, or the spirit

In modern everyday speech, people would usually replace "fleshly" with words like physical, bodily, carnal, or sensual.

Understanding how "fleshly" differs from similar words will sharpen your grasp of it considerably.

Bodily — purely neutral; simply means "of the body." No moral weight at all. ("bodily functions," "bodily harm")

Physical — broad and neutral; can relate to the body or to the material world in general. No moral tone.

Carnal — very close to "fleshly," but more explicit and more negative. "Carnal" zeroes in almost entirely on sexual appetite and is blunter about it. "Fleshly" is slightly softer and broader.

Sensual — relates to pleasure from the five senses. Can actually be positive (a sensual piece of music, a sensual meal). "Fleshly" is more loaded with the body-vs-spirit contrast.

Worldly — similar to the third sense of "fleshly," but "worldly" focuses on society, ambition, and material life, while "fleshly" specifically roots things in the body and its appetites.

At its simplest:Of or relating to the physical body
Most commonly:Relating to bodily desires, especially sexual desire and physical pleasure — often with a moral warning built in
In religious/philosophical writing:Belonging to the earthly, worldly realm as opposed to the spiritual
Rare, literary use:Simply resembling or suggestive of flesh
Tone:Formal, literary, slightly or strongly negative depending on context
Core contrast implied:Body vs. spirit / earthly vs. divine

If you ever encounter "fleshly" and feel unsure, ask yourself: Is this about the body and its desires, being placed against something spiritual or higher? If yes, you're reading it correctly.
6185: Now, here's your complete guide to the word fleur-de-lis:

A fleur-de-lis (plural: fleurs-de-lis) is a specific, highly recognizable decorative symbol that looks like a stylized, three-petaled flower — most commonly described as a lily or iris. It is not a photograph or a realistic drawing of a flower. It is an abstracted, simplified design that has been used for centuries as an emblem, a motif, and a symbol across art, architecture, heraldry, and culture.

Picture a tall central petal pointing upward, flanked by two curved petals bowing outward on either side, and a horizontal band or curved bar wrapping around the base of all three petals, holding them together. The overall shape is symmetrical, elegant, and instantly recognizable. Think of the logo of the New Orleans Saints NFL team, or the symbol on the Quebec flag — both use a fleur-de-lis.
The Two Ways the Word Is Used

The noun fleur-de-lis can refer to two related but slightly different things:

1. The symbol or emblem itself
This is the most common use. When someone says "a fleur-de-lis," they almost always mean the stylized design — used in art, flags, crests, jewelry, ironwork, and decoration. For example: "The gate was decorated with golden fleurs-de-lis."

2. The actual iris flower
Less commonly, especially in older or literary usage, fleur-de-lis can refer to the real iris plant (the flower), since the design was originally inspired by it. This usage is rare in modern everyday English.

You will see fleurs-de-lis in many places:

  • Flags and coats of arms: The flag of Quebec (Canada) has four fleurs-de-lis. The historic royal standard of France was covered in them. Many European royal and noble families used them in their heraldic symbols.
  • Architecture: Churches, cathedrals, fences, railings, and old buildings across Europe and the Americas often feature fleur-de-lis carvings or ironwork at the tips of gates and fence posts.
  • Jewelry and fashion: Rings, necklaces, and brooches shaped like a fleur-de-lis are very common.
  • Sports: The New Orleans Saints (American football) use it as their logo, and it appears in the logos of several other teams and organizations.
  • Scouting: The Boy Scouts of America and the World Scouting movement use a fleur-de-lis as a central part of their badge.
  • Religion: It frequently appears in Christian art and church decoration, often as a symbol of the Virgin Mary.

Over centuries, the fleur-de-lis has come to carry a rich set of meanings:

  • Royalty and nobility: It is most strongly associated with the French monarchy. French kings used it as their royal emblem for centuries, making it a worldwide symbol of aristocratic power and prestige.
  • Purity and virtue: Its association with the lily flower connects it to ideas of innocence, holiness, and spiritual purity.
  • New Orleans and Louisiana: Because Louisiana was a French colony, the fleur-de-lis is deeply embedded in the culture and identity of the region and is considered a local symbol of pride.
  • French heritage generally: Wherever French culture spread — Canada, Louisiana, parts of Africa, the Caribbean — the fleur-de-lis followed as a marker of that heritage.

• "The crown was inlaid with three golden fleurs-de-lis."
  • "She wore a silver fleur-de-lis pendant around her neck."
  • "The iron fence was topped with fleurs-de-lis."
  • "The fleur-de-lis has been a symbol of French royalty for centuries."
The Core Idea, in One Sentence

A fleur-de-lis is a classic, three-petaled decorative symbol shaped like a stylized lily, historically associated with French royalty and nobility, and now widely used in flags, architecture, jewelry, sports, and design to convey elegance, heritage, or cultural identity.
6186: "To flex" means to bend or to tighten. But depending on the context, it takes on quite different shades of meaning.
1. To contract or tighten a muscle

This is the most literal meaning. When you flex a muscle, you actively tighten it — especially to make it visibly stand out. Most commonly done with the biceps (the muscle on your upper arm).

  • "He flexed his biceps to impress everyone at the gym."
  • "The bodybuilder flexed his muscles on stage."

You can flex almost any muscle — your abs, calves, jaw, back. The key idea: you are consciously contracting it, usually to show it off or to engage it for effort.
2. To bend a joint or limb

"Flex" also means to bend a part of your body at a joint. This is common in medical, fitness, and everyday language.

  • "Flex your knees slightly when you land from a jump."
  • "The doctor asked him to flex his ankle to check the injury."
  • "Flex your fingers and wrists before a long typing session."

A small but useful distinction from meaning #1: in #1, you tighten the muscle in place. In #2, you move the joint by bending it. In practice, both often happen together — bending your arm involves both flexing the bicep and moving the elbow joint.

More broadly, flex describes bending any object that can bend without breaking.

  • "She flexed the plastic ruler to test how far it would bend."
  • "He flexed the wire into a circular shape."

This sense is less common in daily speech but appears in technical or descriptive writing.
4. To demonstrate power, strength, or capability

Here, flex leaves the physical world and enters the figurative. The phrase "flex one's muscles" — and often just "flex" on its own in the right context — means to actively put your power, capability, or influence on display. No actual muscles are involved.

This is very common in politics, business, sport, and international affairs.

  • "The country flexed its military muscles by conducting large exercises near the border."
  • "The tech giant flexed its financial muscle by acquiring three companies in a single week."
  • "After winning three matches in a row, the team began to really flex."

The idea: you're not just having power — you're making it visible, often to send a message, intimidate a rival, or assert dominance.
5. To show off or boast (modern slang)

This is the most popular meaning in informal, everyday language today — especially among younger people and on social media. To flex means to show off something you have or can do: your money, your possessions, your achievements, your looks, your lifestyle.

This meaning grew directly out of bodybuilding culture. Bodybuilders "flex" their muscles to show them off. Over time, the word expanded to mean showing off anything at all.

  • "He's always flexing his new car on Instagram."
  • "Stop flexing your grades in front of everyone."
  • "She bought designer clothes just to flex on her classmates."

You'll also hear "flex on someone", which means to show off specifically in front of that person — often to make them feel inferior or to assert your superiority over them.

  • "He flexed on his rivals by scoring 40 points in the game."
  • "She was clearly flexing on her ex with those photos."

Notice what every meaning shares: making something visible through active effort. When you flex a muscle, you make it stand out. When a country flexes its power, it makes that power impossible to ignore. When someone flexes on social media, they push their success right in front of everyone's face.

All roads lead to: deliberate display.
An important distinction: Flex vs. Brag

When someone brags, they talk about how great they are. When someone flexes, they show it — through actions, possessions, or behaviour. Flexing is about demonstration, not just words.

  • Bragging: "I'm so rich."
  • Flexing: Driving up in a Ferrari without saying a word.

In slang usage, "flexing" can carry a mildly negative tone — implying the person is being unnecessarily showy or trying too hard. But it can also be neutral or even admiring depending on context.

  • "He was flexing his wealth all night" → slightly critical; he's showing off more than needed.
  • "She flexed her skills on stage" → neutral or admiring; she delivered an impressive performance.

Context and tone of voice determine which reading is meant.
All five meanings at a glance

1. To tighten or contract a muscle
  2. To bend a joint or limb
  3. To bend a flexible object
  4. To demonstrate power, strength, or authority (figurative)
  5. To show off or boast about something (slang)

The first three are literal and physical. The fourth is metaphorical but professional/formal. The fifth is informal and modern. Knowing which one is meant is usually straightforward from context.
6187:
Flexibility is the quality of being able to change, adapt, or adjust easily — without breaking, failing, or resisting too much.

Think of a fresh green twig from a tree. You can bend it in different directions and it won't snap. That twig has flexibility. Now think of a dry, dead stick. Try to bend it — it breaks immediately. That stick has no flexibility.

This is the heart of the word: the ability to bend and adapt rather than stay rigid and break.
The Two Main Worlds of This Word

"Flexibility" is used in two broad ways — one physical, one non-physical. Both share the exact same core idea, just applied to different things.

1. Physical Flexibility

This refers to how easily a physical object — or a human body — can bend, stretch, or move without breaking or getting hurt.

When used about the body, flexibility means how far your muscles, joints, and limbs can comfortably move and stretch. A gymnast who can do a full split has extremely high flexibility in her legs and hips. Someone who can barely touch their toes has low flexibility. Yoga is one of the most well-known practices for increasing the body's flexibility.

When used about materials or objects, flexibility describes how much something can bend without cracking or breaking. Rubber has high flexibility — you can stretch and twist it easily. Glass has almost zero flexibility — it shatters the moment you try to bend it. A leather belt has moderate flexibility. An iron rod has very little.

So in the physical world, flexibility is simply: how much can this bend before it gives up?

2. Non-Physical Flexibility (the more common everyday use)

This is where the word gets really powerful and widely used. Here, flexibility describes the ability of a person, a plan, a system, a schedule, or an idea to change and adapt depending on the situation.

Flexibility in a person
When we say a person has flexibility, we mean they are willing and able to change their approach, plans, or opinions when the situation demands it. They don't insist on doing things in only one fixed way.

Imagine you plan to meet a friend at 3 PM, but your friend calls and says they can only come at 5 PM. A flexible person would say, "No problem, 5 PM works for me." A rigid (opposite of flexible) person would say, "No, it has to be 3 PM or nothing." Flexibility here is the willingness to adapt and adjust.

At work, flexibility in a person might mean they're willing to take on different tasks, work different hours, try new methods, or change their plan when something unexpected happens. Employers often look for this quality because rigid people struggle when reality doesn't match their expectations.

Flexibility in a schedule or timetable
A flexible schedule is one that doesn't lock you into fixed, unchangeable time slots. For example, a flexible work schedule might let you start work at 8 AM or 10 AM, depending on your preference, rather than forcing everyone to start at exactly 9 AM. There's room to adjust. A rigid schedule has no such room.

Flexibility in rules or policies
Some rules are very strict — you either follow them exactly or you face consequences. Other rules have flexibility built in, meaning they can be applied with some room for judgment depending on circumstances. For example, a school rule that says "no phones in class" with zero exceptions has no flexibility. But if the rule says "no phones in class, except in genuine emergencies," that rule has a little flexibility — it allows for exceptions when the situation truly calls for it.

Flexibility in thinking or opinions
A person with mental or intellectual flexibility doesn't cling to one idea just because it's theirs. If they're shown good evidence or a strong argument, they're willing to reconsider and update their view. They can see things from different angles. The opposite is someone who is mentally rigid — they've made up their mind and no amount of reasoning or new information will change it.

Flexibility in a plan or system
A flexible plan is one that can be adjusted if things change. A project plan that says "if X doesn't work, we'll try Y instead" is a flexible plan. A plan that only has one path and no alternatives has no flexibility — if something goes wrong, the whole plan collapses.

Flexibility almost always carries a positive feeling. When we say someone or something is flexible, we usually mean it as a compliment or a desirable quality. In contrast, the opposites — rigidity, inflexibility, stiffness — usually carry a negative or unfavourable feeling.

However, there are cases where too much flexibility can suggest a lack of principles or reliability. For example, if a politician changes their position on every issue depending on who they're speaking to, you might say they have "too much flexibility" — meaning they stand for nothing firm. Context matters.

Flexibility isn't all-or-nothing. It exists on a spectrum.

  • Full/complete flexibility: Almost total freedom to change and adapt. "The contract gave her complete flexibility to work from anywhere in the world."
  • Some/moderate flexibility: A middle ground — some room to adjust, but not unlimited. "There's some flexibility in the deadline, but not much."
  • Limited/little flexibility: Very little room to change. "The airline has limited flexibility when it comes to refunds."
  • No flexibility / zero flexibility: No room to adapt at all. "The rules were enforced with no flexibility whatsoever."
Common Phrases and Situations Where You'll Meet This Word

• "Flexibility at work" — the ability to adjust your hours, location, or tasks. Many people today value workplace flexibility very highly.
  • "Financial flexibility" — having enough money or financial options so that you can respond to unexpected events or opportunities without being trapped. If you have savings, you have financial flexibility.
  • "Flexibility of approach" — being willing to try different methods to solve a problem rather than insisting on just one way.
  • "Build in flexibility" — deliberately design a plan, system, or schedule to have room for adjustment. "We should build in some flexibility in case the project takes longer than expected."
  • "Lack of flexibility" — the absence of this quality, usually mentioned as a criticism or a problem. "The system's lack of flexibility frustrated many users."
  • "Demonstrate/show flexibility" — to prove through actions that you are willing to adapt. "She demonstrated remarkable flexibility during the negotiations."

These come from the same root and are worth knowing alongside "flexibility":

  • Flexible (adjective): describes the person or thing that has flexibility. "She is flexible." "This is a flexible material."
  • Inflexible (adjective): the opposite — unable or unwilling to bend or adapt. "He is inflexible in his views."
  • Inflexibility (noun): the opposite of flexibility. "His inflexibility cost him the deal."
  • Flexibly (adverb): in a flexible manner. "The team responded flexibly to the changing demands."
Putting It All Together — A Summary in Plain Words

Flexibility means the quality of being easy to bend, change, or adjust. In the physical world, it describes how much a body or material can stretch and move. In everyday life — which is where you'll use this word most — it describes how willing and able a person, a plan, a rule, or a system is to adapt when circumstances change. It is widely considered a strength, both in people and in systems, because the world is unpredictable and those who can adapt tend to succeed where rigid, unyielding things snap and fail.
6188: "Flick" is a versatile word. As a noun, it has several distinct meanings, but they all share a common spirit: something quick, light, and sharp.

This is the core and most common meaning. A flick is a sudden, short, snappy movement — usually made with a finger, the wrist, or a thin, flexible object. It is never slow. It is never heavy. It happens in an instant and stops just as fast.

Think of how a cat lazily bats at a dangling string — that's a flick. Think of how a magician snaps a card off a deck with one finger — that's a flick. Think of how someone turns off a light switch with one fast push of a finger — that's a flick.

Examples:

  • "With a flick of his wrist, the fisherman cast the line far into the river."
  • "She turned off the lamp with a flick of her finger."
  • "The horse chased away the flies with a flick of its tail."

Notice that a flick always involves very little effort and very little distance. The movement is small, but it happens with speed and precision. That combination — small + fast + light — is the soul of a flick.
2. A Light, Quick Hit or Strike

Closely related to the above, a flick can also mean the act of hitting or striking something (or someone) in that same quick, light way — usually with a finger or fingernail.

It is not a punch, not a slap, not a hard hit. A flick is playful, casual, and light. It stings a little, but it doesn't cause serious pain. Parents sometimes do this to children. Friends sometimes do it to each other as a joke.

Examples:

  • "He gave his friend a flick on the ear as a joke."
  • "She flicked a breadcrumb off the table — one quick flick with her finger and it was gone."
3. A Quick Flip or Browse Through Pages

A flick can also describe the action of turning through the pages of a book, magazine, or notebook very quickly and lightly — without reading carefully, just glancing at pages as they go by.

Examples:

  • "She had a quick flick through the magazine while waiting at the dentist's."
  • "He gave the brochure a flick but didn't find what he was looking for."

This meaning carries the same spirit: quick, light, and not deeply invested. You're not reading every word — you're breezing through.

In informal, everyday English — especially in American and British speech — a flick simply means a movie or film. This is slang, but it is widely understood and very commonly used.

Examples:

  • "Do you want to catch a flick tonight?" (= Do you want to watch a movie tonight?)
  • "That was a great flick — I'd definitely watch it again."
  • "It's an old flick from the 1980s, but it still holds up."

You can use this word in casual conversations without any problem. Just don't use it in very formal writing.

In British English, the flicks (always plural, always with "the") refers to the cinema — the place where you go to watch movies, not a single film itself.

Examples:

  • "We're going to the flicks on Friday — want to come?" (= We're going to the cinema.)
  • "I haven't been to the flicks in ages."

This is an older, slightly old-fashioned British expression, but it is still used, understood, and charming.
6. A Small Splash, Mark, or Streak

Less commonly, a flick can also mean a small, thin mark or splash of something — like paint, mud, or ink — that got there because of a quick, uncontrolled movement.

Examples:

  • "There were flicks of white paint on the floor after he finished the ceiling."
  • "Her coat had little flicks of mud on it from the puddle."

You can picture this easily: if you dip a brush in paint and snap it quickly, the paint flies off in small, thin droplets. Each one of those little marks is a flick.
The Big Picture: How All These Meanings Connect

All these meanings of flick are united by the same underlying idea — something that is brief, light, and happens in a flash. Whether it's a movement, a hit, a glance through pages, a film, or a small mark — a flick is never slow, heavy, or labored. It is always quick, sharp, and effortless.

Once you feel that core quality — quick, light, and snappy — you will understand and remember every meaning of this word naturally.
6189:
Flick means to make a quick, light, snapping movement — usually with your fingers, wrist, or a thin object. Think of the motion you make when you snap a crumb off a table. That's a flick. It's fast, it's light, and it involves a small, sharp jerk of movement. Not slow. Not heavy. Just a sudden, effortless snap.

Three things are always true of a flick:

  • It is fast (happens in an instant)
  • It is light (doesn't need much force)
  • It is small and sharp (a quick snap, not a big sweeping motion)

Because the core idea is a "quick, light snap," the word is used in many situations where that kind of motion is happening.

1. To remove or send something away with a quick, light snap

This is the most basic use. You use a finger, thumb, or an object to send something away — lightly and quickly.

"She flicked the crumbs off the table."
"He flicked the fly away from his arm."
"The boy flicked a rubber band across the room."

The thing being flicked is usually small and light. You are not pushing it — you are snapping it away.

2. To operate a switch or button with a quick snap

When you turn a light switch on or off, you do it with a quick, effortless motion — and that's exactly what "flick" captures. It is widely used for switches, buttons, and levers.

"She flicked the light switch on."
"He flicked off the TV and went to bed."
"Just flick the switch on the wall."

The word "flick" here perfectly describes how casually and quickly you do it — it takes almost no effort.

3. To move through something quickly and casually

When you move through pages, channels, or images quickly — without reading or watching carefully — you are "flicking through" them. The idea is the same: light, fast, snapping motion, but now applied to the act of turning pages or changing things rapidly.

"He was flicking through a magazine in the waiting room."
"She flicked through the TV channels, looking for something to watch."
"He flicked through his phone, scrolling past photos."

Notice the word "through" is often used with this meaning.

4. When a body part moves with a quick, sharp snap

Animals — and sometimes people — move their body parts in a sudden, sharp, light way. English uses "flick" for this.

"The cat flicked its tail in irritation."
"The snake flicked its tongue in and out."
"She flicked her hair over her shoulder."

Here, nothing is being sent away — the body part itself is the thing that is making the quick, snapping movement.

5. When someone's eyes or gaze moves suddenly to something

If you quickly look toward something — almost involuntarily — your eyes "flick" to it. The movement of the gaze is sudden and short, just like any other flick.

"Her eyes flicked to the door when she heard the knock."
"His gaze flicked briefly toward the stranger."

6. When a light or image appears or turns on very briefly

When something lights up or appears for a short, sudden moment, it can be described as "flicking on."

"The screen flicked on for a second and then went dark."
"A light flicked on in the upstairs window."
How "Flick" Is Different from Similar Words

This is important, because a learner might wonder: why not just say "push" or "throw" or "brush"?

Similar wordWhy it's different from "flick"
PushPushing is slower and more deliberate. A flick is faster and lighter.
ThrowThrowing involves more force and a longer, bigger motion. A flick is small.
BrushBrushing is a smooth, gentle, sliding motion. A flick is a sharp snap.
