SwatSwatting is heavier and more forceful. A flick is almost effortless.
TapTapping is a gentle touch that usually doesn't send something away. A flick sends things away.

The unique quality of flick is this combination: fast + light + snapping. No other English word captures all three of those things together in one word. That's what makes it special and widely used.

• Flick through — move through pages, channels, or images quickly
  • Flick on / flick off — turn something on or off with a quick motion
  • Flick away — remove something with a quick snap
  • Flick at — send something toward someone/something with a snap
  • Flick one's wrist — make a quick, rotating motion of the wrist (used in sports like tennis or cricket)
One Image to Remember It All

Imagine you have a tiny crumb on your desk. You don't pick it up carefully, and you don't push it slowly. You just touch it with your finger and — snap — it flies off in an instant. That single motion — fast, light, and sharp — is the soul of the word flick. Every meaning of this word, in every situation, comes back to that same idea.
6190: "Flick through" means to turn the pages of something — like a book, magazine, or newspaper — quickly and casually, without reading everything carefully. You are just moving from one page (or item) to the next in a fast, light way to get a general feel for things, not to study them deeply.
Breaking It Down Word by Word

Understanding each word separately makes the whole phrase click.

"Flick" describes a quick, light, snappy movement. Think of flicking a crumb off a table with your finger — it is fast, effortless, and small. When you flick pages, you use your thumb or fingers to rapidly push them from one side to the other. There is nothing heavy or slow about it.

"Through" here means going from one end toward the other — moving across something, cover to cover, start to finish (or at least partway).

Put them together: flick + through = to move quickly and lightly from one page (or item) to the next, without stopping to pay close attention to any single one.

This is important, because "flick through" is not just about speed — it is also about attitude and purpose. When you flick through something, you are being:

  • Casual — you are not in a serious, focused reading mode.
  • Exploratory — you are just looking to see what is there, what catches your eye.
  • Non-committal — you are not sitting down to study; you are browsing lightly.

Imagine you are sitting in a waiting room and you pick up a magazine. You do not read every article word by word. You just quickly flip the pages, glancing at pictures and headlines. That is "flicking through."

Here are clear examples showing the phrase in action:

  • "She flicked through the fashion magazine while waiting for her coffee."
  • "He flicked through the report but did not actually read it properly."
  • "I flicked through the photo album and felt a wave of nostalgia."
  • "She handed him the menu and he flicked through it in about ten seconds."
  • "The teacher flicked through the students' notebooks to check if they had done the work."
It Goes Beyond Books and Magazines

"Flick through" started with physical pages, but it has naturally extended to other things. You can flick through:

TV channels — When you hold a remote control and press the button rapidly to change from one channel to the next, you are flicking through channels. You are not watching any one thing properly; you are just scanning to see what is on.

  • "I spent ten minutes just flicking through channels but nothing looked interesting."

Photos or images — Even on a phone or digital camera, when you swipe quickly through photos one after another, you are flicking through them.

  • "She flicked through the photos on her phone after the wedding."

Flashcards or documents — Any collection of items you can move through quickly, one by one.

  • "He flicked through his revision flashcards the night before the exam."

"Flick through" is a phrasal verb. Here is how it works grammatically:

It is usually used as "flick through + something" (it takes an object).

  • "She flicked through the book."
  • "He is flicking through the channels."
  • "I have flicked through the report."

You can conjugate it like any regular verb: flick / flicks / flicked / flicking / have flicked.

You can also split the phrase in some cases:

  • "She flicked the pages through quickly." (less common, sounds a little stiff)
  • The natural form keeps "flick through" together: "She flicked through the pages." ✓

"Flick through" is more common in British English. Americans often use "flip through" instead, which means exactly the same thing.

  • British: "I flicked through the catalogue."
  • American: "I flipped through the catalogue."

Both are correct and widely understood everywhere. If you are learning British English, "flick through" is your go-to. If you are learning American English, "flip through" is more natural — but knowing both is always an advantage.
How It Compares to Similar Phrases

Several phrases are close relatives of "flick through." Knowing the differences will sharpen your understanding.

"Leaf through" — Almost identical in meaning. You turn pages lightly and casually. "Leaf" refers to the leaves (pages) of a book. It sounds slightly more gentle and leisurely than "flick through," almost poetic.

  • "She leafed through the old letters slowly."

"Thumb through" — Very similar. The word "thumb" highlights that you are literally using your thumb to push the pages. It feels slightly more physical and tactile.

  • "He thumbed through the dictionary looking for the word."

"Skim through" — Here the focus shifts from the physical act of turning pages to the reading itself. When you skim through something, you are reading quickly but you are actually paying some attention to the words — just not reading every single one. "Flick through" can mean you barely read anything at all; "skim through" means you are reading, just rapidly.

  • "I skimmed through the article to get the main idea."

"Browse through" — This has a slightly more purposeful, exploratory feeling. You are looking around with mild interest, possibly searching for something specific. It is also commonly used online (browsing the internet).

  • "He browsed through the bookshop shelves for an hour."

"Glance through" — Emphasises the visual, quick look aspect. Your eyes move over things briefly.

  • "She glanced through her notes before the meeting."

The key difference to remember: "Flick through" is the most physical and mechanical of the group — it focuses specifically on the quick, light, casual action of turning pages or items, often implying the least amount of careful attention.

Picture someone flicking a light switch — fast, effortless, click-click-click. Now imagine doing that same action to the pages of a book. You are not lingering. You are not thinking hard. You are just moving through it — flick, flick, flick.

That image captures "flick through" perfectly.

"Flick through" means to move quickly and casually through pages, channels, photos, or similar items — turning or passing them one by one in a fast, light way — without paying deep or careful attention to each one. It describes both the physical action (light, rapid movement) and the attitude (casual, exploratory, non-thorough). It is used in everyday British English and is equivalent to the American "flip through."
6191:
To flicker means to move, shine, or appear in a quick, unsteady, and repeated way — going back and forth between being there and almost not being there, never quite settling into one steady state.

The most important idea inside "flicker" is instability. Something that flickers is not solid. It is not fixed. It keeps wavering, trembling, or briefly appearing and disappearing. Think of a candle in the wind — it doesn't go fully out, but it doesn't burn steadily either. It dances between bright and dim. That restless, unstable, in-between quality is the soul of this word.
The Three Main Ways "Flicker" Is Used

1. When Light or Flame Flickers

This is the most classic and original use of the word. When a light source flickers, it rapidly and repeatedly shifts between brighter and darker — it trembles, it wavers, it almost dies but comes back.

The candle flickered in the breeze coming through the open window.
The old bulb flickered twice before going out completely.
The campfire flickered and danced in the dark.

Notice that flickering light is never fully off and never fully stable. It lives in the in-between. A light that simply switches off doesn't flicker. A light that blazes steadily doesn't flicker. Flickering is that nervous, restless movement in the middle.

This is also why we use "flicker" for screens, projectors, and monitors when they behave unstably:

The TV screen flickered whenever a truck drove past.

2. When Something Moves Quickly and Lightly

"Flicker" also describes a very quick, light, darting movement — something that moves so fast it almost seems to tremble or flash before your eyes.

A lizard's tongue flickered out and caught the fly in an instant.
Her eyes flickered toward the door when she heard the knock.
The butterfly's wings flickered as it rested on the flower.

Here, the movement is tiny and rapid. It is not a big, slow, heavy movement — it is sharp, quick, and brief. The idea of "barely there" and "gone before you fully register it" is still present.

3. When an Emotion, Thought, or Expression Flickers

This is perhaps the most poetic and powerful use of the word. When an emotion or expression "flickers," it appears briefly, faintly, and incompletely on someone's face or in their mind — and then fades. It was there, but just barely. You almost missed it.

A smile flickered across her face before she turned serious again.
Hope flickered in his chest as he read the letter.
Doubt flickered through her mind for just a moment.
Anger flickered in his eyes, but he said nothing.

This usage beautifully captures those tiny, fleeting, hard-to-catch human feelings — the ones that visit briefly and leave before anyone can comment on them. The emotion was real, but it was fragile and short-lived. It didn't burn steadily; it flickered.
The Core Quality Across All Uses

No matter whether "flicker" is used for light, movement, or emotion, the same core qualities are always present:

  • Quick — it happens fast, not slowly
  • Repeated or brief — it either happens again and again in rapid cycles, or appears just for a flash
  • Unsteady — it is not solid, stable, or constant
  • Small in scale — not dramatic; subtle
  • Not fully there, not fully gone — this is the key feeling. Something flickering exists at the edge of disappearing.
How Flicker Differs From Similar Words

Understanding where "flicker" ends and similar words begin will sharpen your sense of it considerably.

Flicker vs. Flash
A flash is a single, sudden burst — one moment of brightness. A flicker is repeated and unsteady. Lightning flashes. A dying candle flickers.

Flicker vs. Glow
A glow is warm and steady. Embers glow. A flicker, by contrast, is unsteady. These two words are opposites in terms of stability.

Flicker vs. Blink
When a light blinks, it switches cleanly on and off — often in a regular, intentional pattern. A traffic light blinks. When a light flickers, the switching is irregular, involuntary, and nervous — it suggests instability or weakness.

Flicker vs. Shimmer
Shimmering is a soft, gentle, continuous wavering of reflected light — like sunlight on water. It is smooth and almost pleasant. Flickering is more sharp, quick, and suggests fragility or unsteadiness.

Flicker vs. Twinkle
Stars twinkle — this is a gentle, rhythmic, charming kind of wavering. Flickering has more urgency and instability to it; it suggests something is struggling rather than sparkling.
The Emotional Tone of the Word

"Flicker" often carries a feeling of fragility and vulnerability. When something flickers — whether a flame or a hope — it suggests that thing could easily be extinguished. It is alive, but barely. It is holding on. This gives the word a subtle emotional weight that makes it beautiful to use in writing.

The last flicker of faith kept her going through the hardest months.

That sentence works so well precisely because "flicker" tells us the faith was small, unsteady, and in danger of dying — but still there. That is the word's quiet power.

To flicker is to appear, shine, or move in a quick, repeated, unsteady way — never fully stable, never fully gone — whether you are talking about a trembling flame, a darting eye, or a brief and fragile feeling passing through a person's heart.
6192:
Imagine a butterfly in a garden. It lands on one flower, then flutters to another, then to another — never staying anywhere long, never fully settling. Now imagine a person who behaves the same way — with their plans, their moods, their commitments, and their attention. That person is flighty.

A flighty person is someone who is unreliable, unfocused, and hard to pin down. They jump from one idea, mood, plan, or interest to another very quickly, without much thought, and without following through. They are not grounded or steady. You cannot count on them.
What a Flighty Person Actually Looks Like

To make this very concrete, here are the kinds of things a flighty person does:

  • They make plans with you and cancel at the last moment — not once, but as a pattern.
  • They get excited about a new hobby, buy all the equipment, and then completely lose interest within a week.
  • They start sentences, thoughts, or projects and never finish them.
  • Their moods shift quickly and without obvious reason — cheerful one moment, distracted the next.
  • They make big promises and forget them entirely.
  • When you need to have a serious conversation with them, they seem scattered and don't fully engage.
  • They act on whims. If something shiny and new catches their eye, they abandon whatever they were doing before without a second thought.

The key pattern is: no follow-through, no stability, no consistency.
The Tone of the Word — Is It Positive or Negative?

"Flighty" is a mildly negative word. It is a criticism, but a gentle one — it is not a harsh insult. It does not suggest the person is evil or dangerous. It suggests they are irresponsible and immature in the way they handle their attention and commitments.

Think of it on a scale:

Spontaneous → Free-spirited → Flighty → Reckless → Irresponsible

"Spontaneous" is positive — it means you act freely and joyfully. "Free-spirited" is mostly positive. But "flighty" is where the same trait tips into something frustrating and unreliable. It is the point where being free becomes being untrustworthy. "Reckless" and "irresponsible" are stronger and more serious. "Flighty" sits right in the middle — not dangerous, but definitely not a compliment.

If someone calls you flighty, they are saying: "I can't rely on you. You don't take things seriously enough. You drift."
Who or What Can Be Called Flighty?

Mostly people. "Flighty" is almost always used to describe a person's personality or behavior. Historically, it was used more often to describe women than men (as a stereotype), which is worth knowing — you may notice this in older books or films. Today, it can be used for anyone, regardless of gender.

It can also describe someone's behavior in a specific situation, not just their whole personality:

  • "He's been flighty lately" — meaning recently, his behavior has been erratic and unreliable, even if he's not always like that.
  • "She gave a flighty answer" — meaning her response was scattered and hard to follow.

It is rarely used to describe things, objects, or places. It lives almost entirely in the world of human personality and behavior.

Understanding a word clearly also means knowing how it differs from words that look similar.

Flighty vs. Fickle: A fickle person changes their opinions, preferences, and feelings constantly — they liked you yesterday, today they don't; they wanted chocolate, now they want vanilla. Flighty is broader — it covers a person's whole way of operating: their plans, attention, behavior, and follow-through. All fickle people are a bit flighty, but a flighty person is more than just fickle.

Flighty vs. Scatterbrained: A scatterbrained person is disorganized and forgetful — they can't find their keys, they forget appointments, their thoughts are all over the place. This is more about mental disorganization. A flighty person may not be forgetful — they might remember perfectly well that they made a plan with you, but they simply drift away from it because something else caught their interest. Flighty is more about unreliability and lack of commitment, while scatterbrained is more about mental chaos.

Flighty vs. Capricious: Capricious means acting on sudden, unpredictable impulses — often used for people in power who make sudden, whimsical decisions. It has a slightly grander, more dramatic feel. Flighty is more casual and everyday, and emphasizes the lightweight, drifting quality of a person's character.

Here are clean, natural examples of "flighty" in use:

  • "I wouldn't ask her to help organize the event — she's too flighty to be counted on."
  • "He used to be flighty in his twenties, jumping from job to job, but he's much more settled now."
  • "Her flighty nature made it hard for her to finish anything she started."
  • "Don't let her flighty reputation fool you — she takes her art very seriously." (Here it's used to acknowledge the label while pushing back against it.)
  • "The flighty young man had a new obsession every week."
If you had to remember just one thing: a flighty person is someone whose attention, mood, and commitments flutter around like a butterfly — never settling, never reliable, never fully serious.
6193: A flimflam is a trick designed to deceive someone — usually to cheat them out of their money, their trust, or something else valuable. The person running the flimflam pretends something is true when it isn't, and the victim believes it and gets hurt as a result. In short: it's a con, a scam, a swindle.

The word "flimflam" carries two closely related meanings as a noun. They both revolve around deception, but one is about actions and the other is about words.

1. A Deceptive Scheme or Trick (a con/scam)

This is the most common use. A flimflam is a carefully constructed trick — a scheme that lures a person into a false sense of security and then cheats them. It almost always involves some level of cleverness on the deceiver's part. The victim usually walks away having lost money, believing they were part of a fair deal.

"The old man lost his savings to a flimflam — the salesman had promised him a miracle medicine that turned out to be plain water."

"The entire investment opportunity was a flimflam from the start — there was no company, no profits, nothing."

Notice that a flimflam isn't a clumsy lie. It's a constructed deception — something planned, usually with a setup, a false promise, and a payoff for the cheater.

2. Deceptive or Nonsensical Talk

A flimflam can also refer to words or talk that are misleading, hollow, or deliberately confusing — language designed to pull wool over your eyes rather than inform you. This is talk that sounds meaningful or convincing but actually contains no real substance, or is designed to trick you into believing something false.

"The politician's speech was pure flimflam — it said a lot without meaning anything."

"Don't fall for his flimflam. He uses complicated words to confuse you so you stop asking questions."

In this sense, flimflam is very close to words like nonsense, hogwash, or hot air — but with an important difference: flimflam isn't just stupid or wrong, it's deliberately deceptive. The speaker knows it's empty. That's the whole point.

"Flimflam" has a particular feel to it that's worth understanding. It is:

Informal and colorful. You'd use it in everyday conversation, not in a courtroom. If someone cheated you, you might tell the police it was "fraud," but you'd tell your friends it was "a complete flimflam."

Slightly old-fashioned. The word has a vintage charm to it — it calls to mind shady salespeople, travelling circus shows, and snake-oil salesmen from a century ago. That said, people still use it today.

Mildly humorous. Because of the way it sounds, the word carries a hint of irony or wit. Calling something a "flimflam" often signals that you've seen through the trick and you find it almost laughably transparent in hindsight.
The Person Who Does It: A "Flimflam Artist"

One of the most useful phrases built from this word is "flimflam artist" (sometimes "flimflam man"). This refers to the person who runs the flimflam — a skilled, practiced deceiver who makes a habit of tricking others for personal gain. Think of a con artist, a charlatan, or a fraudster with a smooth tongue.

"He was a notorious flimflam artist who had cheated people in three different cities before anyone caught on."
How It Differs from Similar Words

These words are all cousins, but they aren't identical:

  • Scam / Con — Very similar to flimflam, but more modern and neutral in tone. "Flimflam" carries more color and an old-fashioned flair.
  • Fraud — More serious and legal in weight. Fraud is what courts deal with. Flimflam is what people talk about at the dinner table.
  • Hoax — A hoax is meant to fool people, but not always to steal from them (a hoax might just be a prank). A flimflam almost always has a selfish motive behind it.
  • Nonsense — General empty talk. Flimflam specifically implies the emptiness is intentional and deceptive, not just accidental stupidity.

If you remember just one thing: a flimflam is a clever, deliberate deception — either as a scheme that cheats someone, or as talk designed to mislead them. The person behind it knows exactly what they're doing. The victim does not. That gap — between what the deceiver knows and what the victim believes — is where the flimflam lives.
6194:
Flimsy means not strong enough for what it needs to do. It describes something that is too weak, too thin, or too unconvincing — something that fails to hold up when pressure is applied to it, whether that pressure is physical force or logical scrutiny.

Think of it as the opposite of solid and sturdy.

"Flimsy" works in two main areas of life: the physical world and the world of ideas.

Side 1: Physical Weakness

When describing a physical object, "flimsy" means it is poorly built, thin, and fragile — the kind of thing that bends, breaks, tears, or collapses far too easily. It suggests that the material or construction is simply not strong enough to do its job properly.

Examples:

  • "The flimsy cardboard box collapsed under the weight of the books."
  • "She wore a flimsy plastic raincoat that the wind ripped apart in seconds."
  • "The children's tent was so flimsy that a mild breeze knocked it over."
  • "Don't put anything heavy on that shelf — it's flimsy."

In each case, the object looks or feels inadequate. It might be made of cheap material, be too thin, or be poorly assembled. The key idea is: it cannot handle the stress placed on it.

🔑 Think of a house of cards. It looks like a structure, but it has almost no strength. That is the essence of "flimsy" in the physical sense.

Side 2: Intellectual or Logical Weakness

"Flimsy" is also used to describe things that lack substance, depth, or convincing power — such as arguments, excuses, evidence, or reasons. When something is flimsy in this sense, it is easy to doubt, challenge, or see through.

Examples:

  • "He gave a flimsy excuse for missing the meeting — he said he forgot, even though everyone had reminded him twice."
  • "The lawyer argued that the evidence against her client was far too flimsy to prove guilt."
  • "Their plan to double profits in one month was based on flimsy assumptions."
  • "She rejected his flimsy reasoning immediately."

Here, "flimsy" signals that the idea, excuse, or argument does not hold up under thinking or questioning. Just like a weak shelf that collapses under weight, a flimsy excuse collapses the moment someone examines it carefully.

🔑 If someone gives you a flimsy excuse, you probably think: "That's not good enough. I don't buy it."
The Tone: What Feeling Does "Flimsy" Carry?

"Flimsy" almost always carries a critical, negative, or dismissive tone. When you call something flimsy, you are saying it falls short of what is needed or expected. It often implies:

  • Disappointment — "I expected better."
  • Skepticism — "I don't believe this."
  • Criticism — "This is not good enough."

It is not a neutral word. If someone calls your argument "flimsy," they are politely (or not so politely) saying it is weak and unconvincing.

This is where many learners get confused. Let's compare:

Flimsy vs. Fragile:
"Fragile" simply means easily broken — but without any judgment about quality. A beautiful, expensive crystal glass is fragile, but it is not flimsy. "Flimsy" adds the extra idea of poor construction or inadequacy. A flimsy object is fragile because it is badly made or too thin — it was never strong enough to begin with.

Flimsy vs. Thin:
"Thin" is purely about physical measurement — it says nothing about quality. A piece of paper is thin, but we don't call paper "flimsy" unless it's failing to do its job. "Flimsy" goes beyond describing thickness to judging the object's ability to function.

Flimsy vs. Weak:
"Weak" is a broader, more general word. "Flimsy" is more specific and more vivid — it almost always suggests both physical lightness/thinness AND inadequacy at the same time. Calling something "flimsy" paints a sharper, more critical picture than simply calling it "weak."

"Flimsy" is a regular adjective, so it follows standard adjective rules.

Before a noun (attributive position):

  • a flimsy excuse
  • a flimsy structure
  • flimsy evidence

After a verb (predicative position):

  • The excuse was flimsy.
  • The structure looks flimsy.
  • Her reasoning seems flimsy.

Comparative and superlative forms:

  • That excuse is even flimsier than the last one.
  • This is the flimsiest material I have ever seen.

These are the words you will most often see paired with "flimsy" in real life:

  • flimsy excuse — the single most common use
  • flimsy evidence — often used in legal or journalistic contexts
  • flimsy argument / reasoning — in debates or discussions
  • flimsy pretext — a false or weak justification
  • flimsy material / fabric — thin, cheap cloth
  • flimsy structure / construction — a building or object that isn't strong
A Simple Way to Remember It

Imagine a house of cards in a light breeze. It looks like it could be a real structure — but it's not. One small push and it all falls apart. That image — something that looks functional but collapses easily under the slightest pressure — is the soul of the word flimsy, whether you are talking about a poorly built shed or a see-through excuse.
6195:
To flinch means to make a small, sudden, involuntary movement — usually pulling back or tensing your body — as an automatic reaction to something painful, frightening, shocking, or deeply unpleasant.

The three most important words there are small, sudden, and involuntary. You don't plan to flinch. Your body just does it on its own, in a split second, before your brain can even think.
The Physical Sense (the most common use)

This is flinch in its most literal, visible form — a bodily reaction.

  • A doctor moves a needle toward your arm → you flinch, pulling your arm back slightly.
  • Someone swings their hand close to your face as a joke → you flinch, jerking your head away.
  • A firecracker goes off right next to you → you flinch, your whole body tenses and recoils for a moment.
  • You accidentally touch a very hot surface → you flinch, yanking your hand back.

Notice: in every case, the movement is small and brief. You are not running away. You are not screaming. It is just a quick, instinctive recoil — the body's way of trying to protect itself from something that feels like a threat or pain.

Flinch doesn't always mean a visible body movement. It is also used figuratively to describe an internal reaction — a moment of emotional discomfort, hesitation, or shrinking away when faced with something difficult or upsetting.

  • "She didn't flinch when she heard the devastating news." → She showed no visible shock, distress, or emotional wavering. She remained calm and steady.
  • "He flinched at the cruel words." → The harsh words affected him, even if only slightly. You could see it on his face or in his expression.
  • "The soldier flinched when recalling the horrors of war." → Even a tough, experienced person had a brief, involuntary moment of pain or discomfort at the memory.

In this sense, flinch captures that moment when something hits you emotionally and your inner composure breaks — even just for a second.

When you say someone flinches from something, it means they avoid or hesitate to do something because it is hard, painful, or frightening — like a mental form of shrinking away.

  • "A good leader never flinches from making tough decisions." → A good leader faces difficult decisions directly, without avoiding them out of fear or discomfort.
  • "She flinched from telling him the truth." → She hesitated or pulled back from saying something difficult.

Here, flinch carries a slight suggestion of weakness or reluctance — the person is backing away from a challenge they probably should face.

This phrase is used to express that someone did something bold, painful, or difficult with no sign of fear or hesitation whatsoever.

  • "He walked into the burning building without flinching." → He showed zero fear; he did not hesitate for even a second.
  • "She stared at him without flinching." → She held her gaze steadily, without backing down or showing discomfort.
  • "The surgeon performed the delicate operation without flinching." → With complete calm and steadiness, no sign of nerves.

This expression is often used to praise someone's courage or composure.

Understanding what flinching implies will help you use and recognize the word with real precision.

1. It is involuntary. This is crucial. If someone chooses to step back, that is not a flinch. A flinch happens before the person can control it. This is why it reveals true emotion — you cannot fake not flinching, and you cannot always stop yourself from flinching.

2. It signals vulnerability. Because a flinch is uncontrolled, it exposes a person's true reaction. In tense situations — a confrontation, a negotiation, a stare-down — the person who flinches first is seen as the one who cracked under pressure.

3. The trigger is usually negative. You flinch at pain, fear, shock, disgust, or a harsh word. You would not flinch at something pleasant. It is always a reaction to something that feels like a threat — real or perceived.

4. It is brief. A flinch lasts a fraction of a second. If someone pulls away and stays away, that is not a flinch — that is a retreat. The flinch is just that one instantaneous moment of reaction.
How Flinch Differs from Similar Words

These words are close in meaning but not identical:

  • Wince — Very similar to flinch, but wince is almost exclusively about pain (physical or emotional). You wince at a painful memory, at a cringe-worthy joke, at a wound being cleaned. A wince is typically shown in the face — squinting eyes, a tight grimace. Flinch is broader and often involves the whole body.
  • Recoil — Much stronger than flinch. To recoil is to pull back sharply, often with disgust or horror, not just fear. "She recoiled from the rotting smell." Recoil can also feel more deliberate. A flinch is quicker and smaller.
  • Shrink (as in "shrink back") — This implies a more deliberate, ongoing act of making yourself small or pulling away out of fear or submission. Flinch is one sharp moment; shrinking is more of a sustained behavior.

What it isA small, sudden, involuntary movement or reaction
Caused byPain, fear, shock, or something unpleasant
Key qualityUncontrolled — the body or emotions react before you can stop them
Can bePhysical (body) or figurative (emotional/mental)
"Flinch from"To avoid or hesitate doing something difficult
"Without flinching"With complete courage and no hesitation

• Pain: "He flinched as the nurse cleaned the deep cut on his hand."
  • Fear: "The puppy flinched every time someone raised their voice."
  • Shock: "She flinched when the car alarm went off right next to her."
  • Emotional discomfort: "He flinched at the memory of his biggest failure."
  • Courage: "She faced every accusation without flinching."
  • Avoidance: "A true journalist never flinches from reporting the truth, no matter how uncomfortable."

The word "flinch" is quietly powerful — in just one word, it tells you that something was threatening enough to break through a person's composure, even for just a moment.
6196: The word fling has several meanings, but they all share one central idea: something brief, intense, and done without long-term seriousness or commitment. Think of it as something you jump into with energy, enjoy for a short time, and then it's over.
Meaning 1 — A Short Romantic or Sexual Relationship

This is the most common meaning you'll hear in everyday English. A fling is a casual romantic or sexual relationship that is short-lived and not serious. Both people involved usually know from the beginning that it won't last. It is exciting and fun while it lasts, but neither person is planning a future together.

Key qualities:

  • Short in time
  • Exciting or passionate
  • Casual — no deep commitment
  • Temporary by nature — everyone involved knows this

Examples:

  • "They met on a cruise and had a fling. When the trip ended, so did the relationship."
  • "It was just a summer fling — nothing serious."
  • "She wasn't looking for love. She just wanted a fling."

How is a fling different from a relationship?
In a real relationship, both people are committed to each other and think about a shared future. In a fling, there is no such intention. A fling is more like a spark — bright for a moment, then gone.

Common phrase: "summer fling" — This is a very widely used expression. It refers to a casual romance that blossoms during the summer and ends when the season is over. It carries a sense of warmth, fun, and bittersweet endings.
Meaning 2 — A Short Period of Fun, Freedom, or Wild Behavior

A fling can also describe a brief period of doing something enjoyable, carefree, or indulgent — especially before settling into a more serious or responsible phase of life. The idea is of "letting yourself go" or "living freely" for a short time.

Examples:

  • "Before he became a serious politician, he had a fling with music — playing in bands around the city."
  • "She wanted one last fling before the baby arrived, so she went on a trip with her friends."
  • "His fling with gambling ended when he lost too much money."

Common phrase: "one last fling" — This is a very popular expression. It means enjoying yourself freely one final time before responsibilities take over. People often use it before a wedding, a big career change, or a major life event.
Meaning 3 — A Brief, Casual Attempt at Something

A fling can also refer to a short, enthusiastic attempt at trying something out — without any real long-term commitment to it. The person gives it a go, but they are not fully invested, and they usually move on quickly.

Examples:

  • "She had a fling at acting in her twenties but decided it wasn't for her."
  • "He had a fling at writing a novel, but he gave up after a few chapters."
  • "After college, I had a fling at selling real estate before finding my real passion."

Think of it as "dipping your toes" into something. You try it, you experience it briefly, and then you leave.
Meaning 4 — A Physical Act of Throwing (Literal Sense)

In its most literal sense, a fling is a single act of throwing something — usually with force, speed, or carelessness.

Examples:

  • "With a fling of his arm, he sent the stone skipping across the water."
  • "She gave the papers a fling across the desk in frustration."

This meaning is less common in modern everyday conversation. You're more likely to come across it in books, especially older literature. In daily speech, people usually just say "throw" or "toss." However, "fling" as a noun in this sense carries a slight extra quality — it suggests the throw was done with emotion, energy, or carelessness, not with precision.

The Highland Fling is a well-known traditional folk dance from Scotland. It is performed solo (by one person) and is very lively and energetic. The name connects to the physical idea of flinging — the dance involves vigorous, leaping movements.

Example:

  • "The children learned the Highland Fling at the Scottish cultural festival."

You will always see this written as "the Highland Fling" — it is a fixed expression and refers only to this specific dance. You don't need this meaning for everyday English, but it's good to recognize it when you see it.
The Thread That Ties Everything Together

No matter which meaning of fling is being used, the same core idea is always present:

Something brief, energetic, and not meant to last.

A fling is never slow, careful, or permanent. It's a burst — of passion, of fun, of movement. It arrives quickly, feels intense for a moment, and then it's over. That temporary, spirited quality is the soul of this word.

• "have a fling" — to engage in a short romance or a period of fun
  • "summer fling" — a casual romance during summer
  • "one last fling" — a final period of freedom before life gets more serious
  • "a fling at something" — a short, casual attempt at something

To understand "flinty," you need to first picture flint — a rock. Flint is one of the hardest stones found in nature. It is dark grey, extremely dense, and almost impossibly tough. For centuries, people used it to make arrowheads, sharp tools, and cutting edges. Strike a piece of flint against steel and it throws off sparks — it's that hard and resistant. It does not bend. It does not chip easily. It simply holds its ground.

"Flinty" takes all those qualities of flint — the hardness, the toughness, the cold resistance, the unyielding nature — and turns them into a word that describes people, looks, personalities, and attitudes.

Literal meaning (rare): In its most direct sense, "flinty" means made of flint, resembling flint, or containing flint particles. A scientist might describe "flinty rock" or "flinty soil." This is valid but uncommon in everyday writing and speech.

Figurative meaning (very common): This is where "flinty" truly lives. When used to describe a person or their manner, it means tough, cold, and unyielding — emotionally like stone. A flinty person will not melt, will not bend, and will not soften regardless of the pressure or emotion directed at them. They are hard in a quiet, still, immovable way — not loud or explosive, but simply resistant, like the rock itself.
The exact feeling the word carries

This is important: "flinty" is not the same as angry. Anger is hot and loud. Flinty is cold and still. A flinty expression on someone's face is not a scowl of rage — it is a cool, hard, unwavering look that gives nothing away and yields nothing either.

"Flinty" is also not quite the same as cruel. Cruel implies a desire to harm. Flinty is about the absence of softness, not the presence of malice.

The word also carries a certain ambiguity in its tone — it can be slightly negative or quietly admirable depending on context. When someone is described as flinty, they might come across as cold and unfeeling (not great). But they might also be someone who has endured hard things and developed an unbreakable inner toughness because of it — a survivor's quality (admirable). The context around the word tells you which shade is intended.

Eyes and gaze: "Flinty eyes" or "a flinty stare" means a cold, hard, penetrating look that doesn't waver and shows no warmth or sympathy.

Expression and manner: "A flinty expression" or "a flinty reply" suggests someone responding without softness, sentiment, or room for negotiation.

Character and personality: "A flinty character" or "a flinty disposition" describes someone who is fundamentally tough, unsentimental, and not easily moved emotionally.

Determination and resolve: "Flinty resolve" or "flinty determination" means a kind of willpower that is rock-solid and impossible to wear down — here, it's clearly a compliment.

"The old judge looked at the defendant with flinty eyes, unmoved by the tears in the courtroom." — cold and unyielding look.

"Her flinty determination carried her through years of failure before she finally succeeded." — tough, unbreakable resolve; positive.

"He was known as a flinty businessman who never let sentiment get in the way of a deal." — tough, unsentimental, hard to sway.

"Despite the emotional pleas from the crowd, the official gave a flinty response and refused to change the decision." — cold and firm.

In the world of wine, "flinty" is used to describe a particular dry, mineral quality in certain white wines — especially from cool regions of France like Chablis or the Loire Valley. The taste resembles the smell of cold stone or even the faint whiff of a struck match. This is a niche, expert usage, but it comes from the exact same root idea: it reminds you of the cold, hard stone.
Steely, stony, stern, hard, unyielding, implacable, unsentimental, cold, tough, iron-willed.
Warm, soft, tender, gentle, yielding, compassionate, open-hearted, emotional.

"Flinty" is a somewhat literary word. You'll encounter it most in novels, quality journalism, and careful writing. It is not common in casual conversation — though you could absolutely use it there. It has a slightly poetic, old-fashioned quality that makes it feel most natural in written English. When a writer reaches for "flinty" instead of just "hard" or "cold," they are being precise — they want to evoke that very specific image of something that is hard like stone, cold to the touch, and utterly unyielding.

"Flinty" means hard, cold, unyielding, and unsentimental — like flint stone — and is most commonly used to describe a person's character, expression, or determination that refuses to soften, bend, or give way under any pressure.
6198:
Flip means to turn something over quickly with a sharp, light motion. Think of the action — fast, clean, often with a flick of the wrist. A pancake flips when it spins in the air and lands on its other side. A coin flips when you toss it so it rotates before landing. This sudden, complete turning motion is the soul of the word.

Everything else the word means is built on this same idea: a quick, complete change of some kind.

1. To turn something over quickly

The most basic, physical meaning. You flip an object when you rotate or turn it over with speed.

  • "Flip the pancake before it burns."
  • "He flipped the card over to see what was on the back."
  • "Flip the mattress — it'll be more comfortable."

The key detail: flipping is always quick. You don't slowly rotate something — you flip it in one sharp motion.

2. To toss something casually and lightly

When you flip something to someone, you throw it in a relaxed, effortless way — usually a short distance, usually without much force. It suggests ease and casualness.

  • "She flipped the keys to her brother across the room."
  • "The shopkeeper flipped the change onto the counter."
  • "He flipped a coin to decide who would go first."

Flipping a coin specifically means launching it into the air with your thumb so it spins, and then seeing which side faces up when it lands. This is a classic way to make random decisions.

3. To move a switch or lever sharply

You flip a switch, lever, or latch when you move it quickly from one position to another — off to on, closed to open, and so on.

  • "Flip the light switch when you leave."
  • "She flipped the safety switch before starting the machine."
  • "Just flip that lever and the water will start."

One quick motion, and the state of something changes completely.

4. To browse through something quickly

When you flip through a book, magazine, notebook, or TV channels, you move through them rapidly without reading or watching everything carefully. You're scanning, getting a general feel — not studying.

  • "He flipped through the magazine in the waiting room."
  • "She was flipping through channels trying to find something to watch."
  • "I flipped through the report to get the main idea."

You can flip through anything that has pages, sections, or options — physical or digital.

5. To suddenly lose emotional control

When someone flips (or flips out), they suddenly and dramatically lose their temper or composure. They have an extreme reaction — usually anger, but sometimes panic or wild excitement. The suddenness mirrors the physical flip.

  • "My dad is going to flip when he sees this."
  • "She flipped out when the airline lost her bag."
  • "Don't tell him yet — he'll flip."

This is very common in casual spoken English. When someone "flips," their emotional state has turned completely in an instant.

6. To completely change sides or switch allegiance

When someone flips in a situation involving loyalty or position, they turn completely from one side to the other — like a coin landing on its opposite face.

In legal and criminal settings, a criminal who "flips" agrees to cooperate with the police or prosecutors, often testifying against former partners in exchange for a lighter punishment.

  • "The suspect flipped and gave the investigators the names of everyone involved."
  • "The prosecutor spent weeks trying to convince him to flip."

In politics or public opinion, a person flips when they reverse their stated position on an issue — especially if they once held the opposite view.

  • "The senator flipped on the immigration bill after the election."
  • "He used to support the policy, but he's flipped completely."

In both cases, someone who was on "one side" is now on the "other side."

7. To buy something cheap and sell it quickly for profit

This is one of the most common modern uses of the word. When you flip something, you buy it at a low price — often something undervalued, damaged, or unpopular — improve it or wait for the right moment, and then sell it at a higher price for a profit.

Real estate is the most famous example:

  • "They buy rundown houses, renovate them, and flip them for profit."
  • "House flipping became very popular as a way to make money."

But the same idea applies to almost anything:

  • "He flipped old sneakers — buy limited editions cheap, sell them when the price rises."
  • "She flipped used books online."
  • "Traders sometimes flip stocks within hours."

The word captures the speed and the reversal: something goes from low-value to high-value and then changes hands quickly.

8. To perform an acrobatic rotation

In gymnastics, diving, or informal physical activity, to flip means to throw your body through a complete rotation in the air — like a somersault.

  • "The gymnast flipped across the mat and landed perfectly."
  • "He flipped off the diving board into the pool."
  • "She's been learning how to do a back flip."

The body literally "turns over" in mid-air — same core motion, applied to the whole body.

9. A vehicle rolling over

When a car, truck, or boat flips, it rolls over completely — usually in an accident.

  • "The car skidded on the ice and flipped onto its side."
  • "The boat flipped in the storm and everyone had to swim to shore."

Flip through — to browse quickly and lightly
"Flip through the chapter before the lecture."

Flip out — to suddenly lose composure; to go crazy with anger, panic, or excitement
"She flipped out when she found out she'd won."

Flip over — to turn something completely to its other side; or (of a vehicle/object) to roll over
"Flip the steak over now." / "The canoe flipped over in the rapids."

Flip off — (informal, rude) to make a rude gesture at someone by raising the middle finger at them; it's considered very offensive
"The driver flipped off the car that cut him off."

Flip the script — (idiom) to reverse a situation entirely; to turn the tables so that what was working against you now works in your favor
"She was being pressured at the negotiation, but she flipped the script and put them on the defensive instead."

In British English especially, "flipping" (and sometimes "flip") is used as a mild, socially acceptable substitute for a stronger swear word — expressing frustration or surprise without being offensive.

  • "What the flip is going on here?"
  • "That's absolutely flipping ridiculous."

It softens the emotion while still expressing it clearly.

Every single meaning of "flip" shares the same DNA: something changes quickly and completely — a pancake turns over, a switch changes state, a criminal switches sides, a house changes ownership at a profit, a person's emotions go from calm to explosive. The motion is always fast, often decisive, and usually complete.

Once you feel this core — a quick, complete reversal or change — every use of "flip" will make sense naturally, even in sentences you've never seen before.
6199: "Flip off" has two distinct meanings in English. The first is far more common and culturally significant. The second is more literal and straightforward. You need to know both, because context determines which one is meant.
Meaning 1: To Make a Rude Gesture at Someone (Primary Meaning)

This is the most important meaning, and the one you will encounter most often.

When someone flips another person off, they raise their hand and extend only the middle finger (the longest finger) upward while keeping all other fingers curled down. This gesture is deeply offensive and carries a meaning roughly equivalent to saying a very strong, vulgar insult — something along the lines of "I hate you," "Go to hell," or a very rude dismissal.

Why is it called "flipping off"?

The word flip here refers to the quick, sharp motion of snapping or flicking the finger upward. The off suggests directing that gesture away from yourself and at the other person — as if throwing contempt in their direction. So, "flipping someone off" = turning your middle finger sharply toward them.

What emotion does it express?

It expresses a range of strong negative feelings, including:

  • Anger — "You made me furious."
  • Contempt — "I have zero respect for you."
  • Defiance — "I refuse to follow your rules. You can't control me."
  • Dismissal — "I don't care about you at all."

It is never a friendly gesture. Even if someone does it jokingly between very close friends, it is still understood as mock-aggression.

Grammar: How is it used in a sentence?

"Flip off" is a transitive phrasal verb in this meaning, which means it almost always takes an object — the person the gesture is directed at.

Structure: Subject + flip(s)/flipped + off + Object
Or: Subject + flip(s)/flipped + Object + off

Both word orders are acceptable:

  • She flipped off the rude driver.
  • She flipped the rude driver off.

If you use a pronoun (him, her, them, me, us) as the object, the pronoun must go in the middle, between "flip" and "off":

✅ He flipped her off.
❌ He flipped off her. — This sounds unnatural with a pronoun.

Real-life example sentences

  • The cyclist was so angry that he flipped off the car that almost hit him.
  • The teenager got in trouble at school for flipping off her teacher.
  • I can't believe he flipped me off just because I honked my horn!
  • She quietly flipped him off under the table so no one else could see.

Register and Tone

This expression is informal, vulgar, and offensive. You should:

  • Never use it in formal settings — job interviews, business meetings, academic writing, or in front of authority figures.
  • Be careful using it even casually, because it describes a highly offensive act.
  • Use it descriptively (talking about the gesture) rather than as a command directed at someone.

Cultural note

This gesture and phrase are especially common in American English, though it is also widely understood in other English-speaking countries. In some cultures, the equivalent gesture uses different fingers, but the middle-finger meaning of "flip off" is a distinctly North American English expression rooted in American slang.

Related expressions with the same meaning

All of the following refer to the same middle-finger gesture:

  • Give someone the finger — "She gave him the finger."
  • Flip someone the bird — "He flipped them the bird."
  • Give someone the middle finger — more literal and descriptive.
  • Shoot someone the bird — less common, but used in some American regions.
Meaning 2: To Turn Something Off (Secondary Meaning)

This meaning is much more literal. "Flip off" can simply mean to switch something off using a quick flipping motion — usually referring to a light switch, a power switch, or any toggle switch.

The word flip here describes the physical motion of pushing a switch downward or in the "off" direction. Think of a light switch on a wall — you flip it up to turn the light on, and flip it down (or off) to turn the light off.

Example sentences

  • Don't forget to flip off the lights when you leave the room.
  • She flipped off the switch as she walked out.
  • Can you flip off the TV? I'm trying to sleep.

How common is this meaning?

This usage is less common than Meaning 1. Most people simply say "turn off," "switch off," or "flick off" in everyday conversation. You might hear Meaning 2 mainly in casual American spoken English, particularly in certain regions.

Grammar note

Just like Meaning 1, this is also a transitive phrasal verb. The object is the thing being switched off (the lights, the TV, the radio, etc.).

  • He flipped off the generator. ✅
  • He flipped the generator off. ✅
  • He flipped it off. ✅ (pronoun goes in the middle)
How to Tell the Two Meanings Apart

Context makes it almost always obvious:

  • If the sentence is about a person being "flipped off," it is Meaning 1 (the rude gesture). You cannot flip off a lamp at a person.
  • If the sentence is about a machine, switch, or device being "flipped off," it is Meaning 2 (turning it off). You don't give a middle finger to a light bulb.

Compare:

  • "He flipped off his boss." → Rude gesture. He made an obscene middle-finger gesture at his boss.
  • "He flipped off the machine." → He turned the machine off.

Meaning 1Meaning 2
What it meansTo make a rude middle-finger gesture at someoneTo switch/turn something off
Object typeA personA device or switch
RegisterVulgar, informalCasual, informal
How commonVery commonLess common

Because Meaning 1 is so dominant and so strongly associated with this phrase, if you ever use "flip off" in conversation, people will most likely assume you're talking about the rude gesture — unless it's very clear from context that you're talking about a switch. To be safe and avoid misunderstanding, when you mean Meaning 2, it's better to just say "turn off" or "switch off."
